lists.title: 50 Hard-Problem Projects: Search & Systems
lists.author: Arnav Dewan
howToUse: Start with a Starter project in one lane, then grow it into a Hard one rather than jumping between ideas. Good first picks: 1 (recruiter search), 13 (HNSW from scratch), 25 (malloc in C), 33 (crash-safe KV store), 35 (B+tree with a buffer pool).
Levels assume you are learning from scratch: Starter = a few weekends once you know Python or C basics; Intermediate = 1 to 2 months; Hard = open-ended, research-flavored.

Write each one up the way strong systems repos do: (1) one question the project answers; (2) numbers for every claim, with the machine and command that produced them; (3) why the surprising results happened; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.

lanes.name: Search, retrieval & ranking
lanes.intro: Semantic search finds things that sound right but break must-have constraints, and good rerankers are slow and expensive.

lanes.name: Vector search internals
lanes.intro: Keeping recall high while cutting memory, latency and cost, under filters, deletes and constant updates.

lanes.name: Memory & concurrency
lanes.intro: Code that is fast on one thread often collapses on eight, and concurrent code can be wrong in ways tests rarely catch.

lanes.name: Storage & databases
lanes.intro: Data must survive crashes, disks are slow, and every design trades write speed, read speed and space against each other.

lanes.name: I/O, distributed & GPU
lanes.intro: Networks drop and reorder messages, machines fail mid-operation, and GPUs are only fast when memory access is arranged just right.

lanes.name: Bridge: search meets systems
lanes.intro: These combine both lanes, which is where the rarest and best-paid skills sit: making AI and search fast at the systems level.

lists.title: 50 Real-World Projects to Build and Test Outside
lists.author: Arnav Dewan
howToUse: Pick the idea you would actually use this month, then test it outside with real photos, real places and real friends. Your own data is messy in ways public datasets are not, and fixing that is the interesting work.
Start small: a phone camera plus a laptop is enough for most of these; hardware ideas are at the end.
Measure it: accuracy on 100 of your own photos, latency on your phone, or how many friends kept using it after a week.
Privacy rule of thumb: identify things, places, plants and animals, not people. Where people appear, count them anonymously on-device and never store faces.
Safety: for anything about rules or food (fishing limits, allergens), treat the app as a helper and always check the official source.

lanes.name: Hardware & sensors
lanes.intro: These need a Raspberry Pi, an ESP32 or just your phone's sensors, and they exercise the systems lane: small memory, tight latency, unreliable networks.

projects.title: Recruiter search engine on a public resume or jobs dataset
projects.problem: Rebuild the interview pipeline: retrieve, filter, rerank
projects.proveIt: NDCG@10, % of top 10 meeting all hard criteria
projects.question: Can a retrieve, filter, verify, rerank pipeline put only fully qualified candidates in the top 10 while ranking them well by NDCG@10?

steps.title: Frame the recruiter search question and its two metrics
steps.learn: The task mirrors a recruiter search interview: a query mixes hard criteria (must hold) and soft criteria (nice to have). Report NDCG@10 and the % of top 10 results meeting every hard criterion. Data: Kaggle Resume Dataset (2400+ livecareer.com resume examples, 24 categories, uploader-labeled CC0).
verify: Download the CSV and confirm the columns ID, Resume_str, Resume_html, Category and the row count yourself
Read 20 resumes and list which hard criteria the text can actually support (titles, years, degrees, skills)
Write 40 recruiter queries (one hard, one soft criterion each) and freeze 15 as a held-out test set you never look at while building

steps.title: Extract structured candidate profiles from resume text
steps.learn: Hard filters need fields, not prose. Extract normalized title, total years of experience (from date ranges, merging overlaps, treating 'current' roles with a fixed reference date), highest degree and skills. Normalize synonyms (e.g. 'Sr.' and 'Senior') so filters match. Keep 'unknown' distinct from 'no'.

decision.choice: Offline LLM extraction to a strict JSON schema, validated with Pydantic, cached per resume ID
decision.why: The corpus is small (a few thousand resumes), so a one-time LLM pass is cheap, and schema validation catches malformed output. Doing it offline keeps query time fast and makes extraction reproducible from the cache.

alternatives.name: Regex and date rules only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and deterministic, but resume layouts vary a lot and rules miss titles and degrees phrased in unusual ways.

alternatives.name: No extraction, embed raw text
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest pipeline, but you cannot enforce hard criteria, so the % meeting hard criteria will suffer.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. Write extract.py: read the Kaggle resume CSV, call an LLM with a JSON schema (Pydantic model CandidateProfile: title_normalized, years_experience float|None, degree_level enum, skills list[str], evidence spans). Cache results in a JSONL keyed by ID; skip cached rows. Compute years from date ranges in Python, not the LLM, merging overlaps. Tests: overlap merge, 'present' handling with fixed reference date, schema validation failure path.
verify: Hand-check 30 extracted profiles against the raw text and record field-level accuracy for years and degree
Confirm overlapping jobs are not double counted in years of experience on 3 handpicked resumes
Count how many profiles have 'unknown' for each field; note which hard criteria are risky

steps.title: Parse the recruiter query into hard filters and soft criteria
steps.learn: The query parser decides what is non-negotiable. 'Senior accountant, 5+ years, CPA, ideally healthcare' splits into hard filters (title, years >= 5, certification) and soft text ('healthcare'). Values must map onto the same normalized vocabulary used in extraction, or filters silently match nothing.

decision.choice: LLM call with a strict schema whose enum fields reuse the extraction vocabulary
decision.why: Recruiter phrasing is varied and an LLM handles it well, while the schema forces outputs into values the filters understand. Sharing one vocabulary between extraction and parsing removes a whole class of silent mismatches.

alternatives.name: Hand-written grammar
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and free, but only works if queries follow a template; real phrasing breaks it.

alternatives.name: No parsing, treat the query as text
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast to build, but every criterion becomes soft and hard-criteria precision drops.

steps.delegate: Python. parse_query.py with parse(query:str) returning ParsedQuery (Pydantic: hard: list[HardFilter{field, op, value}], soft: str). Use the same enums as extraction. Use tool calling or structured outputs. On validation failure retry once, then fall back to soft-only. Tests: 10 fixture queries with expected hard filters, a fallback test, and an enum-mismatch test.
verify: Hand-label hard vs soft for your 40 queries and measure parser agreement on each field
Feed 5 ambiguous queries ('ideally', 'preferred') and confirm they land in soft criteria
Confirm parser output always validates against the schema, including on a nonsense query

steps.title: Retrieve about 200 candidates with BM25 plus dense vectors
steps.learn: BM25 catches exact skills and certifications (CPA, AutoCAD) that embeddings blur; dense vectors catch paraphrases ('managed payroll' vs 'compensation administration'). Fuse the two ranked lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, which uses ranks rather than raw scores, so the two scales never need calibrating.

decision.choice: rank_bm25 BM25Okapi plus a small sentence-transformers model, brute-force cosine in NumPy, fused with RRF
decision.why: A few thousand resumes fit in memory, so exact search is fast enough and removes ANN recall loss as a variable. Two plain libraries keep the pipeline easy to read and ablate.

alternatives.name: Qdrant with prefetch and RRF fusion
alternatives.tradeoff: Built-in hybrid queries and payload filters; worth it at larger scale or when you need a service, but adds infrastructure to a starter.

alternatives.name: Dense only
alternatives.tradeoff: One index and simpler code, but exact terms like certification names get missed.

steps.delegate: Python. retrieve.py: build BM25Okapi over tokenized Resume_str, embed resumes with a sentence-transformers model (chunk long resumes, max-pool chunk scores per resume), cosine via NumPy. rrf(lists, k) returns fused IDs; return top 200. Save embeddings to .npy with the model name. Tests: RRF on toy lists with known output, deterministic ordering on ties, chunk max-pooling.
verify: Hand-judge the top 20 from BM25, dense and fused for 5 dev queries and count relevant resumes in each (full recall comes after labeling)
Find one query where BM25 wins and one where dense wins and explain why
Confirm the same query returns identical results across two runs

steps.title: Apply hard filters to the candidate pool before ranking
steps.learn: Filtering after taking the top 200 can leave fewer than 10 survivors for strict queries; filtering first guarantees every candidate is eligible. With exact search over a small corpus, pre-filtering has no recall cost, which is not true for ANN indexes at scale.

decision.choice: Pre-filter with boolean masks on extracted fields, then retrieve the top 200 inside the eligible set
decision.why: Exact search makes pre-filtering free, and the prove-it metric punishes any top 10 result that breaks a hard criterion. Masks are simple to test and explain.

alternatives.name: Post-filter the top 200
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but strict queries can end with too few results, hurting both metrics.

alternatives.name: Filter inside a vector DB
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales and handles filtered ANN, but you then depend on the engine's filter strategy and its recall behavior.

steps.delegate: Python. filters.py: apply(parsed.hard, profiles) returning bool mask over NumPy arrays (years >= N, degree_level >= X, normalized title in set, skill contains with fuzzy match threshold). Policy flag for unknown values (exclude or keep-and-mark). retrieve.py accepts the mask. Tests: each operator, unknown handling under both policies, empty-mask path returning an explicit 'no eligible candidates'.
verify: For each dev query, log how many resumes pass the filters; flag queries with fewer than 10
Compare survivors in the top 200 with pre-filter vs post-filter and report the difference
Confirm a resume with 'unknown' years is handled the way your policy says

steps.title: Verify hard criteria with a rule-based checker
steps.learn: Extraction can be wrong, so re-check each hard criterion per candidate against the raw resume text (evidence spans, regex for named certifications, dates re-parsed from the span) and return pass, fail or unknown with the text that justifies it. Rechecking extracted fields alone adds nothing.

decision.choice: Deterministic Python rules over extracted fields plus evidence spans; unknown never ranks above a pass
decision.why: Rules are cheap, repeatable and auditable, which matters when a metric is defined as 'meets all hard criteria'. Pushing unknowns below passes keeps the top 10 clean without discarding them.

alternatives.name: LLM verifier per candidate
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles messy phrasing better, but costs a call per candidate and can disagree with itself across runs.

alternatives.name: Trust the filters only
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra code, but every extraction error reaches the top 10 unseen.

steps.delegate: Python. checker.py: check(candidate, hard_filters) returning list[CriterionResult{field, status: pass|fail|unknown, evidence}]. Recheck against raw Resume_str: confirm each evidence span occurs verbatim, re-parse dates inside it, regex-match named certifications and degrees. Ranking key puts all-pass first. Tests: one fixture per operator, a missing-evidence case returning unknown, and a regression test using the 5 injected violators.
verify: Inject 5 known-violating resumes into a candidate list and confirm the checker rejects all 5
Read the evidence for 20 passes and count how many are actually correct
Report how often the checker disagrees with the metadata filter, and why

steps.title: Rerank eligible candidates on soft criteria with a cross-encoder
steps.learn: Retrieval embeds query and resume separately; a cross-encoder reads them together and scores fit, so it judges 'healthcare billing experience' far better. It is slower, so it only sees surviving candidates. It reads at most 512 tokens per query plus chunk pair, so score the best chunks, not the first page.

decision.choice: sentence-transformers CrossEncoder (ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2) over soft text vs top resume chunks, max-pooled
decision.why: It runs locally on a laptop, is a documented retrieve-then-rerank pattern, and has zero per-query cost, so you can iterate on dev queries freely.

alternatives.name: LLM reranker (pointwise or listwise)
alternatives.tradeoff: Better at nuanced criteria and explanations, but adds latency, cost per query and run-to-run variance.

alternatives.name: bge-reranker-v2-m3
alternatives.tradeoff: A larger multilingual reranker; may score better on varied text, at higher compute per pair.

steps.delegate: Python. rerank.py: rerank(soft:str, candidates, top_n=10) using sentence_transformers.CrossEncoder('cross-encoder/ms-marco-MiniLM-L6-v2'); split resumes into chunks, pick top chunks by BM25 against the soft text, predict pairs in batches, max-pool per candidate; final order keeps the checker's all-pass group first. Tests: deterministic order, batching equals unbatched scores, empty soft text skips reranking.
verify: Hand-judge the top 10 with and without the reranker for 5 dev queries now; compute NDCG@10 for both once the judge-labels step exists
Time reranking 200 candidates on your machine and record the hardware
Read the top 3 for 5 queries and check the soft criterion is actually visible in the text

steps.title: Build graded relevance labels with pooling and an LLM judge
steps.learn: NDCG needs graded labels (for example 0 to 3) per query and resume. Pool the top results from every system variant so no system is judged only on its own hits. An LLM judge scales labeling, but measure how often it agrees with you before trusting it. Keep the dev/test split frozen in step 1.

decision.choice: Pool the top 20 from BM25, dense, hybrid and reranked runs; LLM judge on a 0 to 3 rubric; human-check a sample
decision.why: There are no public relevance labels for this dataset, so you create them. Pooling across variants reduces bias toward one system and a human-checked sample tells you how far the judge can be trusted.

alternatives.name: Label everything by hand
alternatives.tradeoff: Most trustworthy, but slow; realistic only for a smaller query set.

alternatives.name: Use Category as relevance
alternatives.tradeoff: Free labels, but a category is far coarser than a recruiter query, so NDCG would measure the wrong thing.

steps.delegate: Python. labels.py: pool top 20 per query from all runs, dedupe, call an LLM judge on the raw resume with a fixed rubric (0 to 3) plus pass/fail per hard criterion, temperature 0 if supported; write TREC-style qrels and a criteria labels file. CLI to sample N pairs for human labeling and agreement. Load the frozen dev/test IDs. Tests: pooling dedupe, qrels round trip, stable split.
verify: Hand-label 100 pooled pairs and report agreement with the LLM judge
Confirm the judge prompt never sees which system produced the result
Confirm the 15+ held-out queries frozen in step 1 were never used while tuning any earlier step

steps.title: Cache LLM calls and handle failures end to end
steps.learn: Two LLM touchpoints (extraction offline, parsing per query) can fail, rate limit or drift. Caching makes runs reproducible and cheap to rerun; fallbacks keep a query answerable when the parser fails. Record latency per stage so you know where time goes.

decision.choice: Disk cache keyed by hash of model, prompt and input; retry with backoff; soft-only fallback
decision.why: Evaluation means rerunning the same queries many times, so caching removes most cost and variance. A fallback is better than an error for a search tool.

alternatives.name: No cache, call live every time
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but slow, costly and results shift between runs, which corrupts comparisons.

alternatives.name: Async batch every call
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster cold runs at the cost of more complex code; useful once the query set grows.

steps.delegate: Python. llm_cache.py: decorator caching responses in SQLite keyed by sha256(model+prompt+input); retry with exponential backoff on rate-limit errors; per-stage timers written to a CSV. Wire it into extract.py and parse_query.py. Tests: cache hit skips the call (mock client), retry count respected, fallback path on persistent failure.
verify: Run the full pipeline twice and confirm the second run makes zero LLM calls
Simulate a parser failure and confirm results still return using the soft-only fallback
Report p50 and p95 latency per stage over all dev queries

steps.title: Measure it: NDCG@10, hard-criteria precision and ablations
steps.learn: Run every variant on dev and held-out test: BM25 only, dense only, hybrid, plus filters, plus checker, plus reranker. Report NDCG@10 and % of top 10 meeting all hard criteria. Tune only on dev. With about 15 test queries, use per-query paired tests before calling a gap overfitting or a win.
steps.delegate: Python. eval.py: for each variant write a run, load qrels with ranx, compute ndcg@10; compute hard-criteria precision@10 from the independent per-criterion labels (judge plus human sample), not the system's checker. Output a Markdown table for dev and test plus per-query JSON. CLI flags --split and --variant. Tests: toy run with hand-computed NDCG, a variant flag that disables each stage.
verify: Report both metrics for all 6 variants on dev and test in one table
Record machine, OS, Python and library versions, model names and the exact command
Check NDCG on 3 queries with sklearn ndcg_score (add unretrieved judged docs with lowest score) vs ranx 'ndcg'

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: Write the 4-part write-up: the one question, numbers for every claim with machine and command, why surprising results happened (for example where the reranker hurt), and what this does not prove (LLM-judged labels, a synthetic query set, one resume source).
verify: Part 1 states the one question in a single sentence
Part 2 gives a number, machine and command for every claim, for dev and test
Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with an example query
Part 4 lists assumptions, including judge agreement and the dataset's limits

projects.title: HNSW from scratch
projects.problem: Understand the recall / speed / memory triangle by building it
projects.proveIt: Recall@10 vs queries/sec, compared to hnswlib and FAISS
projects.question: How do M, efConstruction and ef trade recall, speed and memory in HNSW, and how close does a from-scratch build get to hnswlib and FAISS?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and dataset
steps.learn: The deliverable is a curve, not a number: Recall@10 (overlap of your top 10 with the exact top 10) against queries per second, one point per ef value. Dataset: sift-128-euclidean from ann-benchmarks (1M train, 10k test, Euclidean, exact top-100 neighbors included).
verify: You can state the one question and the metric pair (Recall@10, single-thread QPS) in one sentence each
You opened the HDF5 file and printed the shapes of train, test, neighbors and distances
You wrote down which three systems will appear on the final plot: yours, hnswlib, FAISS IndexHNSWFlat

steps.title: Build the exact search baseline and recall scorer
steps.learn: Brute force is both the ground truth and the speed floor every ANN index must beat. ann-benchmarks counts a returned neighbor as correct if its distance is within the true k-th distance plus a small epsilon, so ties do not punish you. Your scorer should do the same.

decision.choice: Iterate on a 100k-vector prefix of train with ground truth recomputed by exact search; run final numbers on the full 1M
decision.why: The shipped ground truth is for the full 1M set, so a subset needs its own. A 100k prefix makes a from-scratch build fast enough to rerun many times a day while debugging, and the 1M run then tests that conclusions hold at scale.

alternatives.name: Full 1M from day one
alternatives.tradeoff: Uses the shipped ground truth directly, but every build of a slow from-scratch index costs a long wait, so you debug far less often.

alternatives.name: fashion-mnist-784-euclidean (60k)
alternatives.tradeoff: Small enough to use whole with shipped ground truth, but 784 dims makes each distance costlier and the data is less typical of embedding search.

steps.delegate: Python 3, numpy, h5py, faiss-cpu. Write data.py: load(path, n=None) returns train[:n], test, ground-truth ids and distances; when n is set, recompute exact top-100 with faiss.IndexFlatL2 and take sqrt so distances match the shipped Euclidean ones. Write metrics.py: recall_at_k(found_dists, true_dists, k, eps=1e-3) with the distance-threshold rule; take sqrt of squared-L2 results first. Tests: recall 1.0 for identical, 0.0 for disjoint, ties at the k-th distance count.
verify: Exact search on the 100k subset gives Recall@10 of exactly 1.0 against your recomputed ground truth
Your recomputed top-10 for the full 1M matches the shipped neighbors for a sample of 100 queries
You recorded brute-force QPS on one thread as the floor to beat

steps.title: Choose the language and in-memory layout
steps.learn: HNSW search is pointer chasing: read a node's neighbor list, then fetch those vectors from scattered places. Speed depends on how compactly vectors and adjacency lists sit in memory. SIFT vectors are 128 float32 values, so 512 bytes each before any graph links.

decision.choice: Python with numpy: one contiguous float32 vector matrix plus fixed-width int32 neighbor arrays per layer
decision.why: This is a Starter build whose goal is understanding the triangle, not winning on speed. Contiguous arrays keep distance math vectorized and make memory easy to count exactly, and the gap to hnswlib (C++) becomes a finding you can explain.

alternatives.name: Rust or C++
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick it to compete on QPS with hnswlib; costs more code, and manual memory and concurrency care.

alternatives.name: Python lists of lists for adjacency
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest to write, but per-object overhead hides the true memory cost and slows traversal.

alternatives.name: Numba JIT over numpy arrays
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps Python syntax with much faster loops; adds a compile step and debugging is harder.

steps.delegate: Python 3 + numpy. Create class HNSWIndex(dim, max_elements, M, ef_construction, seed) holding vectors as one float32 array (max_elements x dim), a level per node (int8), layer-0 neighbors as int32 (max_elements x 2M) with a count array, and upper layers as dict level to (ids, int32 neighbor matrix). Add memory_bytes() that sums array nbytes. Tests: memory_bytes matches a hand calculation for small sizes; adding past max_elements raises.
verify: memory_bytes() for 100k SIFT vectors with M=16 matches your hand calculation within 1 percent
You can say how many bytes per node are vectors and how many are graph links

steps.title: Write the distance kernel and count distance calls
steps.learn: Almost all search time is distance computations. hnswlib's l2 space is squared L2, which preserves ranking and skips the square root. Counting distance calls per query gives a hardware-independent cost measure to put next to QPS.

decision.choice: Batch squared L2: compute distances from the query to all unvisited neighbors of a node in one numpy call
decision.why: In Python, one vectorized call over up to 2M neighbors costs far less interpreter overhead than a loop of single distances, and numpy can use SIMD inside the call.

alternatives.name: One distance at a time in a Python loop
alternatives.tradeoff: Mirrors the paper's pseudocode line by line, useful for a first correct version, but very slow.

alternatives.name: Norm expansion |x|^2 - 2x.q + |q|^2
alternatives.tradeoff: Turns batches into a matrix product with precomputed norms; faster for big batches but loses precision for near-equal distances.

steps.delegate: Add distances(q, ids) to HNSWIndex returning squared L2 from q to vectors[ids] as float32 via numpy, and increment a self.dist_count counter by len(ids). Tests: matches a naive per-row loop to 1e-4 relative error on random data; counter increments correctly; empty ids returns an empty array.
verify: Your kernel agrees with faiss.IndexFlatL2 distances on 1,000 random pairs
You measured kernel time for a batch of 32 neighbors with warmup and many repetitions, and wrote down the median

steps.title: Implement greedy beam search on one layer
steps.learn: SEARCH-LAYER (paper alg. 2) keeps a candidate set C (closest first) and a result list W of size ef (furthest first), and stops when the closest unexpanded candidate is further than the furthest result. ef is the beam width that buys recall with distance computations.

decision.choice: heapq min-heap for candidates, negated max-heap for results, visited tracked by a per-query stamp array
decision.why: Two heaps give the paper's two priority queues directly. A stamp array (store the query number per node) avoids allocating a set or clearing a bitmap on every query, which matters when you run 10k queries per ef value.

alternatives.name: Python set for visited
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and fine for a first version; allocation and hashing cost grows with ef.

alternatives.name: Boolean array cleared per query
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast lookups, but clearing N entries each query costs O(N) unless you clear only touched ids.

steps.delegate: Implement search_layer(q, entry_ids, ef, level) in HNSWIndex following alg. 2 of arXiv 1603.09320, returning (dist, id) pairs sorted ascending. Use heapq and a stamp array. Tests: on a hand-built 2D graph, the result equals brute force when ef is at least the graph size; result length is min(ef, reachable nodes); no node is expanded twice.
verify: On a fully connected small graph, search_layer returns the exact nearest neighbors
You can point to the line that implements the early stop and explain why it is safe

steps.title: Insert nodes and assign random levels
steps.learn: Each node gets level floor(-ln(U) * mL). The paper suggests mL = 1/ln(M), which matches a skip list with p = 1/M. Insertion (alg. 1) descends greedily with ef=1 to the node's level, then runs SEARCH-LAYER with efConstruction on each lower layer to pick links.

decision.choice: Paper settings: mL = 1/ln(M), Mmax = M on upper layers, Mmax0 = 2M on layer 0
decision.why: The paper shows these autoselected values as reasonable choices in its parameter plots, and they are what you will compare against. Starting from them means any gap to hnswlib comes from your code, not from different knobs.

alternatives.name: mL = 0 (single layer)
alternatives.tradeoff: A flat navigable graph: simpler, and a useful ablation, but the paper reports losing the logarithmic scaling the hierarchy provides.

alternatives.name: Mmax0 = M
alternatives.tradeoff: Less memory on layer 0, but the paper's Mmax0 plot suggests slower search than near 2M.

steps.delegate: Implement add(vec) in HNSWIndex per alg. 1 of arXiv 1603.09320 with a seeded numpy RNG for levels, entry point update when a new top level appears, bidirectional links, and pruning when a list exceeds Mmax or Mmax0 (call a select_neighbors function, simple version for now). Tests: level histogram roughly geometric with ratio near 1/M; no list exceeds its cap; every link is to a valid id; same seed gives an identical graph.
verify: Level histogram for 100k inserts falls by roughly a factor of M per level
Same seed and data produce byte-identical neighbor arrays on two runs
No neighbor list exceeds Mmax or Mmax0 after building

steps.title: Select neighbors with the diversity heuristic
steps.learn: The simple rule links the M closest candidates. The heuristic (alg. 4) keeps a candidate only if it is closer to the new node than to any neighbor already kept, which spreads links in different directions. The paper reports it helps most at high recall and on clustered data.

decision.choice: Heuristic (alg. 4) with extendCandidates off, keeping the simple rule as a switch for an ablation
decision.why: SIFT is real data, not uniform noise, and high recall is where you will compare against the libraries. The paper sets extendCandidates false by default and describes it as useful only for extremely clustered data.

alternatives.name: Simple: M closest (alg. 3)
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but the paper shows search can get stuck at cluster boundaries and fail to reach high recall.

alternatives.name: Heuristic with extendCandidates on
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for extremely clustered data; adds distance computations at build time.

alternatives.name: keepPrunedConnections on
alternatives.tradeoff: Fills lists back up to a fixed size with discarded candidates; more links and memory per node.

steps.delegate: Implement select_neighbors_heuristic(q_id, candidates, M, extend=False, keep_pruned=False) per alg. 4 of arXiv 1603.09320, used both at insertion and when shrinking full lists. Add a flag on HNSWIndex to choose simple or heuristic. Tests: on two well-separated 2D clusters the heuristic links across clusters while the simple rule does not; output size never exceeds M.
verify: On the 100k subset at a fixed ef, Recall@10 with the heuristic is at least as high as with the simple rule
The two-cluster toy test shows at least one cross-cluster link only with the heuristic

steps.title: Expose k-NN search and the ef knob

projects.title: malloc from scratch in C
projects.problem: How allocators trade speed against wasted memory
projects.proveIt: Throughput and fragmentation vs glibc malloc
projects.question: How much speed and how much wasted memory does each allocator design choice cost, measured against glibc malloc?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metrics and the workloads
steps.learn: Two numbers decide every choice: throughput (malloc/free ops per second) and space utilization. Use CS:APP's verified definition: peak live payload bytes divided by peak heap size (1.0 is perfect). Workloads: mimalloc-bench programs (cfrac, espresso, larson) plus your own trace replays.
verify: Write the question and both metric formulas in your README before any code
Clone mimalloc-bench and the CS:APP malloclab handout; confirm the handout ships only short1/short2 traces
Record the glibc version (ldd --version), CPU model and kernel you will benchmark on

steps.title: Choose how to get memory from the OS
steps.learn: sbrk moves the program break (brk(2) itself says avoid it and use malloc). mmap with MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS returns zeroed, page-aligned memory anywhere in the address space, and munmap can release any region independently. Your allocator carves small blocks out of big OS regions.

decision.choice: mmap large regions (for example 1 MiB arenas) and carve blocks from them; never call sbrk
decision.why: Under LD_PRELOAD other code may also touch the break; mmap regions are independent, can be returned to the OS one at a time, and work the same in a test harness and a preloaded library.

alternatives.name: sbrk-grown contiguous heap
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, matches CS:APP mem_sbrk and lets you coalesce across the whole heap, but you can only shrink from the top and it clashes with anything else using brk.

alternatives.name: One huge mmap reserved up front
alternatives.tradeoff: Contiguous like sbrk without brk conflicts; pages are committed on first touch, but you must pick a maximum heap size in advance.

steps.delegate: In C11, write region.c with void *region_alloc(size_t bytes) and void region_free(void *p, size_t bytes) using mmap(MAP_PRIVATE|MAP_ANONYMOUS) and munmap, rounding up to sysconf(_SC_PAGESIZE). Return NULL and set errno to ENOMEM on failure. Add a unit test that allocates 100 regions, writes every byte, frees them, and checks /proc/self/maps shrinks back.
verify: Run the unit test and show /proc/self/maps before and after: region count returns to baseline
strace -e trace=mmap,munmap,brk: no brk calls come from your allocator (ignore ld.so's startup brk(NULL))

steps.title: Design the block header and alignment
steps.learn: glibc aligns to the larger of 2*sizeof(size_t) and alignof(long double), 16 bytes on x86-64, matching max_align_t: malloc must suit any fundamental type. With sizes rounded to 16, the low 4 bits of the size word are free for flags (allocated, previous-allocated), the boundary-tag trick glibc also uses.

decision.choice: One 8-byte header (size | flags), 16-byte aligned payloads, footer only on free blocks
decision.why: Keeps per-block overhead to one word for allocated blocks, which directly improves utilization on small-object workloads, while a footer on free blocks still lets free() find and merge the previous neighbor.

alternatives.name: Header plus footer on every block
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler coalescing code (the CS:APP textbook start), but costs an extra word per allocated block, which hurts utilization for small sizes.

alternatives.name: Headerless pages with per-page size class
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero per-object overhead (segregated-fit designs), but free() must look up the page metadata and you need size classes first.

steps.delegate: In C, write block.h with inline helpers: hdr_pack(size, flags), blk_size, blk_alloc, prev_alloc, payload_of(block), block_of(payload), next_block, prev_block (valid only when prev is free). Use static_assert for 16-byte alignment. Unit tests: random sizes 1 to 4096 round up correctly, every payload pointer satisfies ((uintptr_t)p % 16) == 0, flags survive size changes.
verify: Hand-draw one allocated and one free block with byte offsets and check it against your code
Unit test shows 0 misaligned payloads across 1,000,000 random sizes

steps.title: Pick the free-list structure and fit policy
steps.learn: An implicit list walks every block; an explicit doubly linked list stores next/prev pointers inside free payloads, so search touches only free blocks. The fit policy (first, next, best) decides which free block serves a request, trading search time against leftover holes.

decision.choice: Explicit free list, first fit, LIFO insertion as the baseline
decision.why: It is the simplest design that is not linear in heap size, and it gives a clean baseline to measure later changes (best fit, size classes) against on the same workloads.

alternatives.name: Implicit list, first fit
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewest lines of code, but every malloc scans allocated blocks too, so throughput collapses as the heap grows.

alternatives.name: Best fit over the whole list
alternatives.tradeoff: Often leaves smaller leftover holes, but scans the full list per request unless you add an ordered structure.

alternatives.name: Address-ordered free list
alternatives.tradeoff: Can reduce fragmentation, but insertion becomes a search, slowing free().

steps.delegate: In C, implement mm_malloc/mm_free on top of region.c and block.h with an explicit doubly linked free list and a fit policy selectable at compile time (-DFIT=FIRST|BEST). Add mm_check() that walks every region and asserts: every free-list entry is marked free, every free block is on the list, no blocks overlap. Call it after every op in debug builds.
verify: Run a 1,000,000-op random trace with mm_check on every op: 0 failures
Compare first vs best fit utilization on the same trace and record both numbers

steps.title: Split oversized blocks and coalesce on free
steps.learn: Splitting returns the unused tail of a large free block to the list (cuts internal waste); coalescing merges a freed block with free neighbors so later large requests fit (cuts external fragmentation). Never split below the minimum free-block size (header, two list pointers, footer).

decision.choice: Split when the remainder is at least the minimum free block; coalesce immediately on free
decision.why: Immediate coalescing keeps the heap invariant simple (no two adjacent free blocks), which makes mm_check strong and the fragmentation numbers easy to explain.

alternatives.name: Deferred coalescing
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster for workloads that free and reallocate the same size (glibc fastbins do this), but footprint can grow and the invariant is weaker.

alternatives.name: Never split
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest path, but every request may waste most of a large block, so utilization drops sharply.

steps.delegate: In C, add split(block, asize) and coalesce(block) covering all 4 neighbor cases (prev/next alloc or free). Maintain the prev-allocated bit in the next block's header. Implement mm_realloc that grows in place when the next block is free. Tests: a scripted sequence hitting each coalesce case, and realloc preserving contents up to min(old,new) size.
verify: mm_check asserts no two adjacent free blocks, passing on 1,000,000 random ops
Show a test where realloc grows in place (same pointer returned) and contents match

steps.title: Add segregated size classes for small objects
steps.learn: Production allocators bucket requests into size classes so a small malloc is a pop from a per-class list instead of a search. Rounding up to a class adds internal fragmentation; class spacing sets that waste.

decision.choice: Segregated free lists: one list per size class for small sizes, the explicit list for the rest
decision.why: Turns the common small-object path into O(1) pops, which is where glibc will beat a single-list allocator on benchmarks like cfrac and espresso; you can then measure exactly what the class spacing costs in utilization.

alternatives.name: Slab pages per size class
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast and headerless, but memory is stuck in a class's pages until the whole page is empty.

alternatives.name: Buddy allocator (power-of-two)
alternatives.tradeoff: Coalescing is cheap, but rounding to powers of two can waste close to half a block.

steps.delegate: In C, add size classes (configurable table, e.g. 16-byte steps to 128, then geometric) with one free list each; requests above the largest class use the explicit list. Expose a debug counter of bytes lost to rounding. Tests: every class boundary size maps to the expected class, mm_check still passes, and a histogram dump of class usage for a trace.
verify: Report utilization and ops/s before and after size classes on the same workload
Measure bytes lost to rounding as a percent of requested bytes

steps.title: Route large requests to mmap and return memory
steps.learn: glibc serves requests at or above M_MMAP_THRESHOLD (128 KiB initially, adjusted dynamically) with their own mmap, so they can be returned independently; the cost is page-rounding waste and a syscall per allocation. Decide when your empty arenas go back to the OS.

decision.choice: Direct mmap for requests above a fixed threshold; munmap an arena when it becomes fully free
decision.why: Large blocks otherwise pin whole arenas and inflate peak RSS, which is the fragmentation number you report. A fixed threshold is easier to reason about than a dynamic one.

alternatives.name: Dynamic threshold like glibc
alternatives.tradeoff: Adapts to programs that repeatedly free large blocks, but makes results depend on history and harder to explain.

alternatives.name: Keep everything in arenas
alternatives.tradeoff: No syscalls on the large path, but freed large blocks never return to the OS.

steps.delegate: In C, mark directly mapped blocks with an IS_MMAPPED flag in the header, munmap them in free, and handle realloc across the threshold. Add an arena-empty check that munmaps the arena. Tests: allocate and free 1,000 blocks of 1 MiB and check RSS returns near baseline via getrusage and /proc/self/status VmRSS.
verify: strace shows one mmap and one munmap per large allocation
VmRSS after freeing all large blocks is within one arena of the starting value

steps.title: Make it thread-safe
steps.learn: malloc(3) is MT-Safe; glibc protects arenas with mutexes and creates extra arenas when it detects contention. A single lock is correct but serializes threads; thread caches avoid the lock on the hot path but hold memory per thread.

decision.choice: One global pthread mutex first, then small per-thread caches per size class
decision.why: The lock makes the allocator correct for real programs under LD_PRELOAD immediately; adding thread caches second lets you measure the speedup on larson and the extra footprint they cost.

alternatives.name: Multiple arenas, thread hashed to arena
alternatives.tradeoff: Like glibc: fewer collisions, but cross-thread frees must find and lock the owning arena.

alternatives.name: Lock-free free lists
alternatives.tradeoff: No lock convoys, but you must handle ABA and safe memory reclamation, which is much harder to get right.

steps.delegate: In C with pthreads, wrap the global allocator in a pthread_mutex_t and register pthread_atfork handlers that take it before fork and release it in parent and child. Add __thread caches (tls_model("initial-exec"), as glibc requires for TLS in a malloc replacement) of up to N blocks per class. Flush a cache on thread exit; pthread_setspecific itself calls malloc, so guard reentry. Tests: 8 threads with cross-thread frees under ThreadSanitizer, and fork from a multithreaded process.
verify: 8-thread stress run of 10,000,000 ops: 0 TSan reports, mm_check passes after join
Record larson ops/s with the lock only and with thread caches

steps.title: Interpose with LD_PRELOAD and test on real programs
steps.learn: glibc supports replacing malloc via LD_PRELOAD interposition. Provide malloc, free, calloc and realloc; a general replacement should also provide aligned_alloc, posix_memalign, memalign, malloc_usable_size and others. free must preserve errno, and malloc must not call glibc code that allocates (fopen, dlopen, stdio).

decision.choice: Build a shared library (libmymalloc.so) exporting the full glibc replacement set
decision.why: mimalloc-bench runs allocators through LD_PRELOAD, so this is how you get an apples-to-apples comparison with glibc on unmodified programs.

alternatives.name: Trace-driven harness only (mdriver style)
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and easy to debug, but misses real programs' calloc, realloc and alignment calls.

alternatives.name: Static linking into each benchmark
alternatives.tradeoff: No interposition surprises, but needs rebuilding every program and hides missing symbols.

Set errno=ENOMEM on failure; save and restore errno in free. Tests: LD_PRELOAD it into ls, python3 -c, and a git clone; a C test for calloc overflow returning NULL and posix_memalign(4096) alignment.

projects.problem: Writes must survive a crash at any instant

projects.question: Can a simple log-based key-value store lose zero acknowledged writes no matter when the process is killed?

steps.title: Frame the question, the guarantee and the test
steps.learn: Define the guarantee: once put() returns success, the write survives a crash. Prove it: 1,000 random SIGKILL runs with zero lost acknowledged writes. No dataset is needed: generate keys and values from a seeded RNG so every failing run can be replayed exactly.
verify: Write the durability contract in one sentence in your README before coding
Write down what counts as loss: an acknowledged key missing or holding an older or garbage value
Record the OS, kernel version and filesystem type (e.g. ext4) you will test on

steps.title: Decide when a write is acknowledged
steps.learn: write(2) returning does not mean data is on disk; only fsync(2) (or O_SYNC/O_DSYNC) does, and fsync blocks until the device reports completion, including flushing a disk cache. fdatasync skips metadata not needed to read the data back, but file size changes still count.

decision.choice: Acknowledge only after the log record is fsynced; batch concurrent puts into one fsync (group commit)
decision.why: The prove-it target is zero loss of acknowledged writes, so ack must wait for durability. Group commit recovers most of the throughput that per-write fsync throws away.

alternatives.name: fsync on a timer (e.g. every 100 ms)
alternatives.tradeoff: Much higher throughput, but a crash loses the last window of acked writes, so it fails this project's guarantee.

alternatives.name: Open the log with O_DSYNC
alternatives.tradeoff: Each write(2) becomes durable on return without separate calls; you can still batch by issuing one big write per batch, but cannot separate writing from syncing.

steps.delegate: In Rust or C, define the API: open(dir), put(key, value), get(key), delete(key), close(). put returns only after the record is durable. Implement a group-commit writer: callers enqueue records, one thread writes the batch with a single write and calls fdatasync, then wakes all waiters. Tests: 16 threads x 10,000 puts, assert number of fsyncs is far below number of puts.
verify: Count fdatasync calls with strace -c -f during a 16-thread run, record puts per fdatasync, and cross-check with an in-process counter
Measure puts/s with group commit vs one fsync per put

steps.title: Frame log records with length and checksum
steps.learn: Recovery must tell a complete record from a torn or garbage tail. LevelDB frames each log record with a CRC32C of type and data, a length, and a type, inside 32 KB blocks. A checksum over the whole record lets the reader stop at the first record that does not verify.

decision.choice: Record = crc32c(4) | length(4) | type(1) | key_len | key | value, all little-endian
decision.why: Self-describing records let recovery detect a partial final write by a short read or checksum mismatch without any extra index, and the type byte encodes put vs delete (tombstone).

alternatives.name: LevelDB-style 32 KB blocks with fragments
alternatives.tradeoff: Corruption is skipped by jumping to the next block boundary, but writing fragments adds complexity.

alternatives.name: No checksum, length only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but a torn tail with a plausible length is replayed as garbage data.

steps.delegate: Write record.rs (or record.c) with encode(record) returning bytes and decode(buf) returning Ok(record, consumed), Incomplete or Corrupt, using the crc32c crate (Rust) or a tested CRC32C table (C). The CRC covers every byte after it, length included; reject lengths above a max record size. Property tests: round-trip for random records; every strict prefix returns Incomplete; no single flipped bit ever returns Ok (a length flip may give Incomplete).

steps.title: Create files durably, including the directory
steps.learn: fsync(2) on a file does not guarantee its directory entry reached disk; an explicit fsync on a descriptor for the directory is needed. So a new log file can vanish after power loss even if its data was fsynced. Apply this every time you create, rename or delete a file.

decision.choice: After creating or renaming any file: fsync the file, then open the directory O_RDONLY and fsync it
decision.why: This is the step most hand-written stores get wrong, and ALICE found crash vulnerabilities in widely used systems from subtle update-protocol assumptions. It costs one extra fsync per file event, which is rare.

alternatives.name: Preallocate a fixed set of log files once
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer directory changes at runtime, but you still need the directory fsync at setup and must handle reuse.

alternatives.name: Rely on the filesystem's journaling order
alternatives.tradeoff: May work on one filesystem, but persistence properties differ across Linux filesystems.

steps.delegate: Add a fs_util module: create_durable(dir, name), rename_durable(dir, from, to), fsync_dir(dir). Each returns errors, never ignores them. steps.title: Decide what to do when fsync fails
steps.learn: After a write-back error the kernel may have dropped the dirty pages and marked them clean, so retrying fsync can report success while data is lost. PostgreSQL's default is to PANIC on a failed data flush and recover from the WAL.

decision.choice: Any write or fsync error is fatal: fail the batch, abort, and after restart append only to a fresh log file
decision.why: An unacknowledged failure is allowed by the contract; a retried fsync that falsely succeeds would silently break it. Crashing reuses the recovery path you already test 1,000 times.

alternatives.name: Retry fsync
alternatives.tradeoff: Looks robust, but may report success for data the kernel already discarded.

alternatives.name: Mark store read-only
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps serving reads, but writers stall and you need a second recovery path.

steps.delegate: In the group-commit writer, on any write or fsync error: return an error to every waiter in the batch, log the errno, and abort the process. Test with a fault-injection wrapper that fails the Nth fsync with EIO and asserts no waiter in that batch receives success.
verify: Injected EIO test: 0 waiters in the failed batch get success

steps.title: Recover by replaying the log and truncating torn tails
steps.learn: On open, read the log from the start, apply each valid record to the index, and stop at the first Incomplete or Corrupt record. A bad record at the tail is an expected torn write; truncate it so new appends never follow garbage. A bad record followed by valid ones means real corruption.

decision.choice: Replay logs in order; truncate an invalid final batch; refuse to open if corruption precedes a later complete batch
decision.why: Truncating the tail is safe because a torn record was never acknowledged. Refusing on mid-log corruption avoids silently dropping acknowledged writes, which is exactly the loss you are proving does not happen.

alternatives.name: Skip corrupt records and continue
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more data available, but can silently lose or reorder acknowledged writes.

alternatives.name: Checkpoint the index periodically
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster recovery on big logs, but adds a second file whose own crash safety must be proven.

steps.delegate: Implement recover(dir): list log files by sequence number, decode records, rebuild the index, ftruncate the last file to the end of the last valid record and fsync it. Tests: append N records, cut the file at every byte offset in the last record, reopen, assert exactly N-1 records and no error; corrupt a middle record and assert open fails.
verify: Cut-at-every-offset test passes for at least 3 record sizes
Recovery time for a 1 GB log is measured and recorded

steps.title: Choose the in-memory index
steps.learn: Bitcask keeps a keydir: a hash table from every key to the file, offset and size of its latest record, so a read is one lookup plus one disk read. The cost is that all keys must fit in RAM and recovery must rebuild the table.

decision.choice: Bitcask-style hash map: key to (file id, offset, length)
decision.why: The project is about durability, not range scans; a hash index keeps the read path trivial so the crash tests stress the log, not the index.

alternatives.name: Sorted map (BTreeMap)
alternatives.tradeoff: Enables range scans and ordered compaction output, at the cost of O(log n) lookups.

alternatives.name: Values in memory too
alternatives.tradeoff: No disk read on get, but RAM bounds the dataset and recovery rereads everything.

steps.delegate: Implement the keydir as a HashMap<Vec<u8>, Loc>. put updates it only after the record is durable; delete inserts a tombstone record and removes the key. get reads with pread at the stored offset and re-verifies the record CRC. Tests: model-based test comparing against a plain in-memory HashMap over 1,000,000 random ops.
verify: Model-based test: 0 mismatches over 1,000,000 random ops
get detects and errors on a value corrupted on disk after write

steps.title: Compact with write, fsync, atomic rename
steps.learn: The log grows with overwritten values and tombstones. Compaction writes only live records to a new file. rename(2) atomically replaces the target for other processes; on journaling filesystems like ext4 a crash leaves the old or new name, and it is durable only after you fsync the directory.

decision.choice: Compact closed files to tmp, fsync it, rename to final name, fsync dir, then delete inputs
decision.why: Every crash point leaves a recoverable state: before rename the tmp file is ignored and deleted on open; after rename both old and new may exist and replay order must make that harmless.

alternatives.name: Rewrite the log in place
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra disk space, but a crash mid-rewrite destroys data.

alternatives.name: Manifest file naming live files
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales to many files, but the manifest itself needs the same atomic update protocol.

steps.delegate: Implement compact(): pick closed log files, write live records to NNN.compact.tmp (keep tombstones while any older file may hold the key), fsync, rename_durable to a sequence number that replays after its inputs and before the active log, update the keydir, delete inputs and fsync the dir. On open, delete any *.tmp. Tests: inject an abort at each step (5 points) and assert recovery yields the same key/value set as before compaction.
verify: Abort-at-each-step test passes for all crash points
Disk usage after compacting a log with 90% overwrites is measured and recorded

steps.title: Build the kill -9 crash-test harness
steps.learn: SIGKILL cannot be caught, blocked or ignored, so the process stops at an arbitrary point and user-space buffers are lost. But data already handed to write(2) stays in the kernel page cache, so kill -9 does not test lost unsynced data or missing fsyncs: a store with no fsync could pass.

decision.choice: Parent spawns writer, records acks over a pipe, SIGKILLs at a random time, reopens and checks every ack
decision.why: Acks are the contract, so the checker needs the exact set of acknowledged writes from outside the killed process. Seeding delay and workload makes any failing run reproducible.

alternatives.name: Power-loss simulation with LazyFS
alternatives.tradeoff: Drops unsynced data (clear-cache) and tears writes, which kill -9 cannot; needs FUSE and is slower per run.

alternatives.name: VM hard reset
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real power loss, but each run takes much longer and is hard to automate 1,000 times.

steps.delegate: Write crashtest (Rust or Python): for run in 1..1000 with seed s: start writer (puts with values derived from key+seq, prints key,seq to a pipe after each ack), sleep a seeded random time (also sometimes during compaction), kill -9, reopen, verify every acked key has its latest acked seq or a later unacked one and no value fails its derivation. Write failing seeds to a file.
verify: 1,000 runs, 0 lost acked writes, with seed list saved
Prove the checker works: disable fsync and use LazyFS clear-cache, or break framing, and see it fail
Confirm some kills landed mid-compaction (log counts)

steps.title: Measure durability cost and recovery time
steps.learn: Measure put throughput and p50/p99 latency for: no fsync (unsafe baseline), fsync per put, group commit at 1, 4, 16 threads; plus recovery time vs log size. Pitfalls: page cache hiding reads, drive write caches, measuring only averages, and a closed-loop client that hides queueing.
steps.delegate: Write bench (Rust or C) with an open-loop generator at a fixed request rate, recording per-op latency into an HDR histogram, for each durability mode and thread count. Output CSV with mode, threads, ops/s, p50, p99, p99.9. Add a recovery benchmark that times open() for logs of 100 MB, 1 GB and 4 GB after dropping caches.
verify: Table of ops/s and p99 for each mode, with device model and filesystem recorded
Record the exact commands and whether the drive has a volatile write cache
Recovery time vs log size plotted or tabulated

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim (runs, loss count, throughput, p99) with machine and command; (3) why surprising results happened; (4) assumptions and limits: kill -9 is not power loss, drives with volatile caches can lie, one filesystem only.
verify: Part 1 states the one question
Part 2: every number cites the machine, filesystem and command
Part 3 explains at least one surprise with evidence (strace, profile, test)
Part 4 says plainly what kill -9 runs do not prove about power loss

projects.problem: Leveled vs tiered compaction trade write, read and space amplification
projects.proveIt: All three amplification numbers per strategy

projects.title: B+tree with a buffer pool
projects.problem: Which pages to keep in RAM (clock, LRU-K, 2Q)
projects.proveIt: Hit rate and throughput per eviction policy
projects.question: For a disk-backed B+tree, which eviction policy (CLOCK, LRU-K, 2Q) keeps the right pages in RAM, measured by hit rate and throughput?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the workload
steps.learn: A buffer pool is a cache of fixed-size pages between RAM and disk. With a B+tree on top, the root and inner pages are hot and leaves are mostly cold. You will compare policies by hit rate (hits / page requests) and ops/s at several pool sizes, on one recorded, skewed trace.

decision.choice: Synthetic YCSB-style workloads (point reads, inserts, short scans) over a generated key set, replayed as a trace
decision.why: No public dataset is needed to study page replacement; what matters is the access pattern. YCSB's documented workload mixes give named, reproducible patterns, and a recorded trace lets every policy see the identical request stream.

alternatives.name: Real DB page-access traces
alternatives.tradeoff: More realistic, but hard to find with a clear license and you cannot vary skew or scan mix to explain why a policy wins.

alternatives.name: Run YCSB against an existing database
alternatives.tradeoff: Tests a whole engine, not your policies; buffer pool effects get mixed with logging, locking and the OS cache.

verify: Write the question, the two metrics and the pool sizes (as a percent of index pages) you will test in one paragraph
Name the 3 or 4 workload mixes you will run and what each is meant to stress (skew, scans, inserts)
Pick the machine and storage device now and record CPU, RAM, disk model and OS version

steps.title: Build fixed-size pages and a disk manager
steps.learn: Everything above the disk manager speaks page ids; it maps page_id to a file offset (page_id * page size) and reads or writes whole pages. CMU's BusTub uses 4 KB pages. The OS page cache will silently absorb your misses unless you bypass it or count misses yourself.

decision.choice: 4 KiB pages in one file, pread/pwrite at page_id * 4096, optional OS cache bypass (O_DIRECT or F_NOCACHE)
decision.why: Fixed 4 KiB pages keep frame math trivial and match the reference course. Positional reads need no shared file cursor, so threads can share one fd. Bypassing the OS cache makes a buffer pool miss cost a real device read, so throughput differences between policies show up.

alternatives.name: mmap the file and let the OS manage it
alternatives.tradeoff: Least code, but the CMU notes list the costs: no control over eviction or flush order, stalls on page faults, SIGBUS on I/O errors. It also removes the thing you want to study.

alternatives.name: Larger pages (8 or 16 KiB)
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher fanout and fewer levels, but fewer frames for the same RAM and more bytes read per miss. Worth a later ablation.

alternatives.name: Buffered I/O only
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler and no alignment rules, but misses become OS cache hits and throughput gaps between policies shrink or vanish.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a DiskManager with read_page(page_id, &mut [u8; 4096]), write_page(page_id, &[u8; 4096]), allocate_page() and sync(). Use pread/pwrite (std::os::unix::fs::FileExt). Add a bypass flag: open with O_DIRECT on Linux (4096-aligned buffers), or call fcntl(fd, F_NOCACHE, 1) on macOS. Count reads and writes. Tests: round-trip 10k random pages, reopen file and reread, allocate past end of file, concurrent reads from 8 threads.
verify: Write 1,000 pages with known patterns, restart the process, and confirm every page reads back byte-identical
With cache bypass on, confirm a cold random page read takes device-level time (time 10k reads) and compare to bypass off
Confirm the read and write counters match the number of calls in a scripted test

steps.title: Build the buffer pool: frames, page table, pins, dirty bits
steps.learn: Frames are a fixed array of page-sized buffers. The page table (in-memory hash map) maps page_id to frame. Each frame has a pin count (pinned frames can never be evicted) and a dirty flag (must be written back before reuse). If every frame is pinned, a fetch must fail, not block forever.

decision.choice: A Replacer trait (record_access, set_evictable, evict, remove) behind the pool, plus RAII page guards that unpin on drop
decision.why: This is the interface CMU's BusTub uses, so you can swap CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q without touching the pool, and every policy sees the same calls. Guards make forgotten unpins (the most common bug, which slowly starves the pool) impossible in normal code paths.

alternatives.name: Hard-code one policy into the pool
alternatives.tradeoff: Less indirection, but each new policy means editing pool logic, and comparisons get confounded by incidental code differences.

alternatives.name: Manual pin/unpin calls
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to a C design and explicit, but leaks are easy; you would need a pin-leak check in every test.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement BufferPool<R: Replacer> over the DiskManager: new(num_frames), fetch_read(page_id), fetch_write(page_id), new_page(), flush_page, flush_all. Use a HashMap page table, a free list, per-frame pin count and dirty flag, and a single pool Mutex for now. Return guards that unpin on Drop and mark dirty on write. Count hits and misses. Tests: pinned pages never evicted, dirty page written before frame reuse, error when all frames pinned, hit/miss counts on a scripted sequence.
verify: Run a test that pins every frame and confirm the next fetch returns an error instead of evicting or hanging
Modify a page, force its eviction, refetch it, and confirm the change survived (dirty write-back works)
Hand-trace a 10-request sequence on a 3-frame pool and confirm the hit and miss counters match your trace

steps.title: Implement LRU and CLOCK as baselines
steps.learn: LRU evicts the least recently used page. CLOCK approximates it with one reference bit per frame and a sweeping hand that clears set bits and evicts the first clear one. Both suffer sequential flooding: one large scan pushes out the hot pages. That weakness is what LRU-K and 2Q target.

decision.choice: Exact LRU (hash map plus list) and CLOCK (reference bit plus persistent hand), both skipping pinned frames
decision.why: LRU is the reference point every paper compares against, and CLOCK is the cheap approximation many systems use. Having both shows whether CLOCK's approximation costs hit rate on your workloads before you add smarter policies.

alternatives.name: Only CLOCK as the baseline
alternatives.tradeoff: Less code, but you cannot separate the cost of approximating LRU from the cost of LRU's own blind spots.

alternatives.name: Random eviction as an extra floor
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial to add and a useful sanity floor; on its own it says little about real policies.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement LruReplacer and ClockReplacer for the Replacer trait. CLOCK: Vec of (ref_bit, evictable), hand index kept between evictions, set ref bit on access, skip non-evictable frames, return None if nothing evictable. Tests: textbook CLOCK example sequence, all-pinned returns None, a scan of N+1 distinct pages over N frames evicts the hot page under both policies (flooding).
verify: Reproduce a small CLOCK example by hand and confirm the evicted frames match the code
Show sequential flooding: hot page plus one scan larger than the pool, and confirm the hot page is evicted under LRU and CLOCK
Measure ns per evict call for each policy at 10k frames with a microbenchmark

steps.title: Implement LRU-K with backward k-distance
steps.learn: LRU-K (O'Neil, O'Neil and Weikum) evicts the frame whose K-th most recent access is oldest, its backward K-distance. Frames with fewer than K accesses get infinite distance; ties go to the earliest access. A page touched once by a scan therefore leaves before a page touched repeatedly.

decision.choice: K = 2, history kept per frame, eviction by scanning or a priority queue keyed by the K-th timestamp
decision.why: The 2Q paper reports that O'Neil et al. found LRU-2 got most of the benefit. K = 2 already separates once-touched scan pages from re-referenced ones, and it is what CMU's project uses as a target.

alternatives.name: K = 3 or more
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs more history before a page earns protection, so it reacts more slowly to a shifting hot set; worth one ablation run.

alternatives.name: K = 1 (plain LRU)
alternatives.tradeoff: No history overhead, but no scan resistance; this is your baseline already.

alternatives.name: Approximate LRU-2 with young and old lists
alternatives.tradeoff: The CMU notes describe this cheap two-list approximation; constant-time, but it is closer to 2Q than to true LRU-K.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement LruKReplacer(k, num_frames): per frame a VecDeque of the last k logical timestamps, an evictable flag; evict picks max backward k-distance, infinite for fewer than k accesses, ties broken by earliest recorded access; remove clears history. Start with O(n) scan, then add a BTreeSet index. Tests: the CMU-style scenario with inf ties, set_evictable changes size, scan pages evicted before twice-touched pages.
verify: On a sequence where a hot page is read twice and then a scan runs, confirm LRU-2 keeps the hot page while LRU evicts it
Confirm ties among infinite-distance frames evict the one with the earliest access
Compare ns per access for the O(n) and indexed versions at 1k and 100k frames

steps.title: Implement 2Q with A1in, A1out and Am
steps.learn: 2Q (Johnson and Shasha) admits new pages to a FIFO A1in. Pages pushed out of A1in leave only their id in a ghost queue A1out. A page re-referenced while its id is in A1out enters Am, an LRU queue. The paper reports LRU-2-like hit rates with constant work per access.

decision.choice: Full 2Q with the paper's suggested sizes: Kin about 25% of frames, Kout holding ids for about 50% of frames
decision.why: These are the values the paper says work well, so you test 2Q as published before tuning. Constant-time updates also make the throughput comparison against LRU-K fair: any hit-rate tie becomes a CPU-cost question.

alternatives.name: Simplified 2Q (from the same paper)
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer moving parts, but the paper notes it needs tuning and adapts less well; use it as an ablation.

alternatives.name: Tune Kin per workload
alternatives.tradeoff: The paper also ran Kin at 20% and 30%; tuning can win a few points but risks fitting your own trace.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement TwoQReplacer(num_frames, kin_frac=0.25, kout_frac=0.5): A1in FIFO of frames, A1out bounded FIFO of page ids (ghosts, no data), Am LRU of frames. On a miss whose page id is in A1out, admit to Am; else to A1in. Evict from A1in if over Kin, else from the Am tail; skip pinned frames. Tests: correlated re-reference stays in A1in, ghost hit promotes to Am, scan pages never reach Am.
verify: Confirm a page read twice within A1in is not promoted, and one re-read after leaving A1in (ghost hit) goes to Am
With A1in already above Kin, confirm a long one-pass scan evicts only A1in pages and every Am page stays resident
Confirm per-access cost stays flat as frame count grows 1k to 100k

steps.title: Lay out B+tree nodes in pages and implement search
steps.learn: Each node is one page. Inner pages hold m sorted keys and m+1 child page ids (first key slot unused); leaves hold sorted keys, values and a next-leaf page id. Every node except the root stays at least half full. Search pins one page per level, binary-searches it, unpins, and descends.

decision.choice: Fixed-size u64 keys and u64 values (record ids), header with type, size and max_size, binary search inside a node
decision.why: Fixed-size entries make node capacity a constant you can compute from 4 KiB, so fanout and tree height are predictable, which you need to reason about which pages a policy should keep.

alternatives.name: Slotted pages with variable-length keys
alternatives.tradeoff: Needed for string keys; adds slot directories and prefix compression, and makes fanout depend on data.

alternatives.name: Store full tuples in leaves
alternatives.tradeoff: Saves a second lookup, but fewer entries per leaf, more leaves, and a different hot-set shape.

steps.delegate: In Rust, define InternalPage and LeafPage views over a [u8; 4096] (zero-copy, little-endian, no padding surprises): header {page_type, size, max_size}, leaf next_page_id. Implement BPlusTree::get(key) that fetches pages only through the BufferPool and holds at most one pin per level while descending. Tests: max_size computed from page size, binary search edge cases, get on an empty tree and a hand-built 2-level tree.
verify: Compute leaf and inner capacity by hand from 4096 bytes and confirm max_size in code matches
Confirm a point lookup on a 3-level tree touches exactly 3 pages (check the pool's request counter)
Confirm no pins remain after 10k lookups (pool pin total returns to zero)

steps.title: Insert with splits and range scans over leaf links
steps.learn: When a leaf overflows, split it in two, copy the middle key up to the parent, and link the new leaf into the sibling chain. When an inner node overflows, split it and push the middle key up; a root split grows the tree by one level. Range scans find the first leaf, then follow next-leaf links.

decision.choice: Insert with splits; deletes as tombstones in the leaf with no merging
decision.why: The study is about caching, and the workloads are reads, inserts and scans. Merge and redistribute logic is the hardest part of a B+tree and does not change which pages are hot. CMU's own leaderboard notes suggest tombstones for deletes.

alternatives.name: Full delete with merge and redistribution
alternatives.tradeoff: A complete structure that shrinks, but much more code and test surface for little effect on this experiment.

alternatives.name: Bulk load sorted keys bottom-up
alternatives.tradeoff: Fast and makes full leaves for the initial load; you still need splits for later inserts. Good as an extra for setup.

steps.delegate: In Rust, implement BPlusTree::insert(key, value) with leaf split (copy up), inner split (push up), and new root on root split; delete as a tombstone flag; scan(start, end) returning an iterator that holds one leaf pin at a time and follows next_page_id. Tests: 1M random inserts then compare every key with a BTreeMap, scans match BTreeMap ranges, tree invariants (sorted, half full, equal leaf depth) checked after every 10k inserts.
verify: Run 1M random inserts and confirm every get and every range scan matches a BTreeMap oracle
Run the invariant checker: all leaves at the same depth, every non-root node at least half full
Confirm a 1,000-key range scan reads only the expected number of leaf pages

steps.title: Add only the concurrency the experiment needs
steps.learn: Policy cost shows up under threads: LRU-K updates history on every access, 2Q and CLOCK do constant work. Latch crabbing lets B+tree operations release a parent latch once the child is safe; leaf scans need no-wait sibling latching to avoid deadlock. You may not need it to answer the question.

decision.choice: One pool latch plus a tree reader-writer lock; hit rate single-threaded, throughput at 1, 2, 4, 8 threads
decision.why: Hit rate does not depend on threads if the trace is fixed, so single-threaded replay keeps it exact. A coarse lock is enough to see whether a policy's bookkeeping becomes the bottleneck as threads grow, without weeks of crabbing bugs.

alternatives.name: Latch crabbing (optimistic version)
alternatives.tradeoff: Real parallelism on the tree and closer to production, but deadlock and pin-leak risk; needs ThreadSanitizer and long stress tests.

alternatives.name: Shard the pool by hashing page id
alternatives.tradeoff: Cuts pool latch contention, but each shard runs its own policy on a slice of frames, which changes hit rates.

steps.delegate: In Rust, wrap the pool state in a Mutex and the tree in a RwLock (reads shared, inserts exclusive). Add a multithreaded driver that splits a trace across N threads. Tests: 8-thread mixed workload for 60 s with an oracle check at the end, pin total returns to zero, run under loom for the replacer or with ThreadSanitizer via cargo +nightly.
verify: Run the 8-thread stress test for 10 minutes with no panic, deadlock or oracle mismatch
Confirm single-threaded replay of the same trace gives the identical hit count twice in a row
Profile the 8-thread run and note what share of time is spent holding the pool latch

steps.title: Build a skewed workload generator and trace replayer
steps.learn: Skew decides everything: with Zipfian keys a small hot set gets most requests. YCSB's Zipfian generator follows Gray et al. (SIGMOD 1994) with constant 0.99, and a scrambled variant scatters hot keys across the key space so they do not sit in the same leaves. Mixing in scans tests flooding.

decision.choice: Zipfian (scrambled and clustered) plus uniform and scan-heavy mixes, written to a trace file of key-level operations
decision.why: Scrambled vs clustered hot keys change how many leaf pages are hot, which is the exact thing eviction must find. Replaying one trace file per mix removes random-number noise from policy comparisons.

alternatives.name: Uniform keys only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to reason about, but leaf hits then track pool size over leaf count for every policy, so policies differ only in keeping inner pages; you learn little.

alternatives.name: Port YCSB's generators exactly
alternatives.tradeoff: Best comparability with published YCSB numbers, at the cost of porting Java code instead of writing a small generator.

steps.delegate: In Rust, write a workload generator: Zipfian per Gray et al. (theta configurable, default 0.99), a scrambled variant (hash the rank), uniform, and a mixer for read/insert/scan ratios with scan length. Output a binary trace (op, key, len). Add a replayer that drives the tree from a trace. Tests: empirical rank-frequency of 10M samples follows the target slope, same seed gives the same trace hash.
verify: Plot rank vs frequency on log-log axes for 10M draws and confirm it is a straight line near the chosen theta
Confirm the share of requests going to the top 1% of keys for each mix and write it down
Confirm the same seed produces a byte-identical trace file

steps.title: Measure hit rate and throughput per policy
steps.learn: Run the matrix: policy (LRU, CLOCK, LRU-2, 2Q) by pool size by workload. Hit rate comes from counters on a single-threaded replay and is exact. Throughput needs warm-up, cache bypass, repeated runs and a recorded command. An offline clairvoyant policy, computed from the trace, gives a ceiling.

decision.choice: Report hit rate after warm-up and median ops/s over 5 runs, with cache bypass on, plus p99 per-op latency
decision.why: Hit rate isolates the policy's choice; ops/s shows whether bookkeeping cost eats the gain. Medians over repeated runs and a fixed warm-up remove the first-run cold cache and noisy-neighbor effects that otherwise decide the ranking.

alternatives.name: Hit rate only
alternatives.tradeoff: Deterministic and cheap, but hides that LRU-K's per-access work can lose on throughput when hit rates are close.

alternatives.name: Leave the OS page cache on
alternatives.tradeoff: Closer to some real systems (PostgreSQL uses it), but OS cache hits mask pool misses; report it only as a separate configuration.

steps.delegate: Write a benchmark harness (Rust binary plus a Python plotting script) that runs every policy x pool size (1%, 5%, 10%, 25% of index pages) x workload, discards a warm-up prefix, records hits, misses, disk reads and writes, ops/s and p99 latency to CSV with git commit, machine and command line. Plot hit rate vs pool size per workload and ops/s vs threads.
verify: Confirm LRU and LRU-2 hit rate never falls as pool size grows (a drop is a bug); small dips for CLOCK or 2Q are possible, investigate large ones
Confirm run-to-run spread of ops/s is under 5% for the 5 repeats, or report the spread
Record the exact command, commit, CPU, RAM, disk model and OS in the CSV header
Run perf (or a sampling profiler) once per policy and note where time goes

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command; (3) why the surprising results happened, for example why 2Q matched LRU-2 or why CLOCK lost under scans; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: The write-up states the one question in its first paragraph
Every claim has a number with the machine, commit and command that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with evidence (a counter, a trace slice or a profile)
An assumptions section says what this does not prove (synthetic traces, one device, coarse locking, no deletes)
