projects.title: Neighborhood menu search
projects.problem: "Spicy vegetarian under $15, open now"
projects.concepts: Hybrid search with hard filters, the same pattern as your interview task
projects.tryIt: Index menus from 30 local restaurants and try it with friends
projects.question: Can hybrid search with hard filters answer 'spicy vegetarian under $15, open now' correctly for 30 real local restaurants?

steps.title: Frame the menu search question and how you will judge it
steps.learn: One query like 'spicy vegetarian under $15, open now' carries three hard filters (diet, price, opening hours) and one soft-ish preference (spicy). The corpus is yours: 30 local restaurants, so there is no public label set. Success means no top 5 result breaks a hard filter, and friends find something they would order.
verify: Pick the 30 restaurants and record for each the menu source URL or photo and the date collected
Write 20 test queries from real cravings before building, each with at least one hard filter
Define 'success' for a friend session in one sentence before anyone tries it

steps.title: Digitize 30 menus into item rows
steps.learn: Menus arrive as websites, PDFs and photos. Each item becomes a row: restaurant, section, name, description, price, plus the raw source. Prices are where errors hurt most, because 'under $15' is a hard filter, and OCR misreads digits. The corpus is small enough to review every price by hand.

decision.choice: Vision-language model extraction to a JSON schema, then a human review pass over every price
decision.why: Menus have columns, icons and odd layouts that a VLM reads more robustly than plain OCR; with roughly a thousand items, a full human price review is a one-evening job and removes the riskiest error.

alternatives.name: Classical OCR plus parsing
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs offline and free, but menu layouts make line-to-price pairing fragile.

alternatives.name: Type menus manually
alternatives.tradeoff: Perfectly accurate and fine for 30 menus, but slow to refresh when menus change.

steps.delegate: Python. ingest.py: for each source (image, PDF, URL) call a VLM with a schema MenuItem{restaurant_id, section, name, description, prices: list[{label, amount_cents}], marks: list[str], source_page} and save JSONL plus the source path. Add review.py, a CLI that shows each item next to its source page and lets me fix the price. Tests: schema validation, price parsing ('$12', '12.50'), multi-price items.
verify: Hand-check every extracted price against the source for 5 restaurants and record the error count
Confirm multi-price items (sizes, add-ons) keep all variants
Count items per restaurant and spot-check any menu with suspiciously few

steps.title: Tag diet and spice with provenance, not guesses
steps.learn: 'Vegetarian' is a hard filter, so you need to know whether the menu says it (a V mark, a veg section) or a model inferred it from ingredients. Store each tag as yes, no or unknown plus its source (stated or inferred). Spice can be a level from chili marks or words like 'hot' or 'Sichuan'.

decision.choice: Tri-state tags (yes, no, unknown) with provenance; only stated or high-confidence inferred tags pass the hard filter
decision.why: Diet is a trust problem: a wrong 'vegetarian' answer is worse than a missing one. Provenance lets the UI say 'marked vegetarian on menu' vs 'likely vegetarian', and lets you tighten the filter later.

alternatives.name: Boolean tags inferred by an LLM
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest and more coverage, but you cannot tell stated facts from guesses.

alternatives.name: Stated marks only
alternatives.tradeoff: Safest, but many menus mark nothing, so most truly vegetarian dishes disappear.

steps.delegate: Python. tag_items.py: rules for stated marks (V, VG, chili icons, section names) first; LLM fills only missing tags with a schema {vegetarian: yes|no|unknown, spice_level: 0..3|null, confidence}; write provenance per field. Tests: rule tags override LLM, unknown stays unknown when confidence is low, re-running is idempotent.
verify: Compare inferred vegetarian tags with stated marks on restaurants that have both; report disagreements
List 10 items tagged vegetarian by inference only and judge each by hand
Confirm every item has a provenance field for diet and spice

steps.title: Model opening hours so 'open now' is correct
steps.learn: 'Open now' is the hard filter most likely to be wrong. Hours have split shifts, spans past midnight, holiday exceptions and a local time zone. Decide whether 'open' means the door is open or that the kitchen takes orders for at least, say, 20 more minutes.

decision.choice: Weekly interval table per restaurant (overnight spans, date exceptions), evaluated in Python with zoneinfo
decision.why: The whole app stays in one Python codebase with one SQLite file, and 30 restaurants is few enough to enter and test hours by hand. Writing the check yourself forces you to test the tricky cases explicitly.

alternatives.name: OSM opening_hours strings plus opening_hours.js
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles split shifts, overnight spans and holidays with a maintained parser (getState), but it is a JavaScript library, so it adds a second runtime.

alternatives.name: Google Place Details opening hours
alternatives.tradeoff: Fresher hours with less manual entry, but needs an API key, has usage costs and terms.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11. hours.py: is_open(intervals, exceptions, tz_name, at, min_minutes_left) and minutes_until_close(...), converting 'at' to the restaurant's zone with zoneinfo.ZoneInfo. Intervals are (weekday, open, close) where close may be past midnight. Tests: split shift, span past midnight, min_minutes_left near closing, a closed-holiday exception, a DST-change day.
verify: Test 'open now' at 10 hand-picked times including just before close and after midnight
Confirm the time zone comes from the restaurant location, not the server clock
Compare stored hours with the restaurant's own site for 10 restaurants and log mismatches

steps.title: Parse the craving into filters plus free text
steps.learn: Turn 'spicy vegetarian under $15, open now' into {diet: vegetarian, max_price: 15.00, open_now: true, spice_min: 1, text: ''}. Decide whether 'under $15' is strict, and which price counts when an item has sizes. Synonyms matter for a small vocabulary: 'veggie', 'meatless', 'hot', 'chili'.

decision.choice: Deterministic regex for price and time words, plus a small LLM call for diet, spice and cuisine
decision.why: Price and 'open now' are high-stakes and easy to parse with rules, so they should not depend on a model. The LLM handles the fuzzy parts where a mistake only costs relevance.

alternatives.name: Rules only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and predictable; feasible with a small vocabulary but misses phrasing friends actually use.

alternatives.name: LLM only
alternatives.tradeoff: Least code, but a misparsed price silently breaks the most important filter.

steps.delegate: Python. parse.py: parse_price(q) and parse_open_now(q) via regex, parse_soft(q) via an LLM with a JSON schema {diet, spice_min, cuisine, text}; merge with rule results taking priority. Synonym table for diet and spice words. Tests: '$15', 'under 15 bucks', 'less than $15.50', 'veggie', no-filter query, LLM failure falls back to rules.
verify: Run all 20 test queries and hand-check every parsed filter
Confirm the regex catches every price phrasing in the 20 queries and no price words leak into the LLM text field
Confirm a query with no filters still returns text-ranked results

steps.title: Index items in SQLite with FTS5 plus a small embedding model
steps.learn: About a thousand short item rows is tiny. Keyword search catches dish names ('paneer', 'mapo tofu'); embeddings catch intent ('something like a burrito bowl'). Fuse both with RRF. Exact cosine over all items is fast enough, so no ANN index is needed.

decision.choice: One SQLite file: FTS5 with bm25() for text, embeddings stored as blobs and scored exactly, fused with RRF
decision.why: Everything (items, hours, tags, index) ships as one file, the hard filters are plain SQL, and the corpus is small enough that exact vector scoring costs little.

alternatives.name: sqlite-vec extension
alternatives.tradeoff: Vector search inside SQL queries; useful if the corpus grows, adds a native extension.

alternatives.name: Qdrant or another vector DB
alternatives.tradeoff: Strong payload filtering and scale, but a server is overkill for 30 restaurants.

steps.delegate: Python. build_index.py: SQLite tables items, restaurants, item_fts (FTS5 over name, description, section); embed item text with a small sentence-transformers model, vectors as blobs. search(text, candidateIds): quote each token and join with OR for MATCH, ORDER BY bm25() ascending, RRF-fuse with cosine. Tests: idempotent rebuild, dish name ranks first, multi-word and punctuation queries, RRF on toy lists.
verify: Confirm a dish name query returns that dish first
Find a paraphrase query that FTS5 misses and the hybrid finds
Time a full query on a phone-class or laptop CPU and record the machine

steps.title: Apply hard filters first and explain empty results
steps.learn: Filter in SQL first (price, diet, open now), then rank only survivors. With a small corpus this is exact and cheap. The common failure is not wrong results but no results: at 10pm few places are open. Relax filters in a fixed, stated order and tell the user what was relaxed.

decision.choice: Strict SQL WHERE on hard filters, then an explicit relaxation ladder (e.g. 'opens in 20 min') with a visible note
decision.why: Friends trust the app only if hard filters always hold; when nothing matches, saying why and offering the nearest option is more useful than silently loosening a filter.

alternatives.name: Post-filter the ranked list
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler, but can return few or no results, and hides why.

alternatives.name: Soft penalties for filter misses
alternatives.tradeoff: Never empty, but a $17 dish can outrank a $14 one, breaking the user's explicit constraint.

steps.delegate: Python. query.py: build SQL WHERE from parsed filters (min variant price < max_price, vegetarian = yes with allowed provenance, is_open at now), pass candidate IDs to search(). If empty, try a fixed ladder (open within 30 min, then price +10%), returning which step applied. Tests: each filter alone, ladder order, message text matches the applied step.
verify: Confirm no top 5 result for the 20 test queries violates price, diet or hours
Run the main query at a late hour and check the relaxation message is accurate
Log how many test queries return zero results before relaxation

steps.title: Rank survivors with simple features and limit repeats
steps.learn: Among eligible dishes, a useful order mixes text relevance, spice strength when asked, and walking distance. Without a cap, one restaurant with ten curries fills the screen. With little data and no labels, a hand-tuned score is honest; a learned ranker would be fitting noise.

decision.choice: Weighted score of fused relevance, spice match and distance, max 2 items per restaurant
decision.why: Few items and no relevance labels mean simple, explainable weights are the right tool; the per-restaurant cap fixes the most visible problem cheaply.

alternatives.name: Cross-encoder reranker
alternatives.tradeoff: Better text matching on longer descriptions, but menu items are short, so gains may be small.

alternatives.name: Learning to rank
alternatives.tradeoff: Needs many labeled clicks; with a handful of friends it would overfit.

steps.delegate: Python. query.py: compute open restaurant IDs with hours.is_open, then build SQL WHERE from parsed filters (min variant price < max_price, vegetarian = yes with allowed provenance, restaurant_id IN open IDs). If empty, try a fixed ladder (opens within 30 min, then price +10%, never diet), returning which step applied. Tests: each filter alone, ladder order, message matches the applied step.
verify: Confirm no restaurant appears more than twice in the top 5
Check distances against a map for 5 restaurants
Ask 2 friends to rank 5 results by hand and compare with the app order

steps.title: Handle stale prices, wrong hours and reports
steps.learn: Menus and hours change, and a wrong 'open now' sends a hungry friend to a closed door. Show when each price and hours entry was last checked, and let users flag wrong data in one tap so you can fix it.

decision.choice: Store collected_at per menu and hours; show it in results; one-tap 'this is wrong' log
decision.why: With 30 restaurants you can re-verify by hand, but only if you know what is stale and where users found errors.

alternatives.name: Scheduled re-scrape of websites
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps data fresher, but breaks on site changes and many menus are photos.

alternatives.name: Ignore staleness
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but silent wrong answers erode trust quickly.

steps.delegate: Python. Add collected_at and hours_checked_at columns, render 'as of <date>' in results, and an endpoint POST /report {item_id, kind} that appends to a reports table with a timestamp and no user identifiers. Tests: report stored without user data, stale threshold marks entries older than N days.
verify: Confirm every result shows the date its menu was collected
Submit a 'wrong info' report and confirm it is logged with item ID and timestamp only
Re-check 5 restaurants a month later and log what changed

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app identifies dishes and places, not people. Query logs from friends need consent and no names; round or drop location. Vegetarian tags and any ingredient info are a helper only: anyone with dietary restrictions or allergies must confirm with restaurant staff, and the app must say so.
verify: Confirm logs hold query text, time and item IDs only, with no names, contacts or precise location
Confirm the result screen tells users to confirm diet and allergens with staff
Confirm no allergen-free claim appears anywhere in the UI
Ask permission before publishing any restaurant's digitized menu

steps.title: Test it outside with friends
steps.learn: Give 5 to 8 friends the app at real meal times with a few scripted queries and their own cravings. Measure what matters here: hard-filter violations in the top 5 (verified against menus or on arrival), sessions where they found something they would order, zero-result queries, and time to a decision.

Report the share of sessions where the friend found a dish they would order
Report zero-result and relaxed-result query counts, and time to decision
Visit or call 3 'open now' results to confirm they were actually open

steps.title: Write it up: question, numbers, surprises, limits
steps.learn: Write the 4-part write-up: the one question, numbers for every claim with machine and command (violations, success rate, latency), why surprising results happened (for example hours errors or late-night empty results), and what this does not prove (30 restaurants, a few friends, one neighborhood).

Part 3 explains at least one surprising result with a real query

projects.title: Lost-and-found matcher
projects.problem: Found items rarely get back to owners
projects.concepts: CLIP embeddings to match a found-item photo to lost reports
projects.tryIt: Run it for a campus or office lost-and-found
projects.question: Can CLIP embeddings put the right lost report in the top 5 for a found-item photo, so staff check a handful of reports instead of all of them?

steps.title: Frame the question, metric and data
steps.learn: Success is ranking: for each found photo, is the true lost report in the top 5 (Recall@5), and how high (MRR)? Offline data: Stanford Online Products (120k images of 23k products, several photos per product) stands in for found photo vs owner photo. Text reports you collect and label yourself.
verify: You wrote the one question and the two metrics (Recall@5, MRR) in your README
You downloaded the dataset and counted products with at least two images
You drafted 30 short text lost reports for real objects you can photograph, labeled to their photos

steps.title: Design the lost report and found item records
steps.learn: Matching uses two kinds of signal: hard facts (when and roughly where it was lost or found, a coarse category) and soft similarity (what it looks like). Contact details are needed to return the item but never needed for matching, so they live apart from everything the matcher reads.

decision.choice: Structured fields (date window, zone, category) plus a free-text description and an optional owner photo
decision.why: Owners rarely have a photo of a lost umbrella but can describe it, so free text is the main query. Date and zone fields are cheap, reliable filters that shrink the candidate list before any model runs.

alternatives.name: Free text only
alternatives.tradeoff: Easiest form to fill, but you lose reliable filters and must guess dates and places from prose.

alternatives.name: Strict category dropdowns, no ML
alternatives.tradeoff: Fully predictable and private, but 'black bag' matches dozens of items and staff still check them all.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, FastAPI, SQLite via sqlmodel. Tables: lost_report(id, description, category, zone, lost_from, lost_to, photo_path nullable, contact_id), found_item(id, photo_path, category, zone, found_at, status), contact(id, name, email) in a separate table the matcher never queries. Pydantic validation: lost_from <= lost_to, zone from a fixed list. Tests: invalid date windows rejected; matcher module has no import of contact.
verify: You can create a lost report and a found item through the API and read them back
A grep shows the matching code never references the contact table

steps.title: Choose the image and text embedding model
steps.learn: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder so matching image and caption pairs land close in one shared space. That lets a found photo be compared directly with a typed description, and with an owner's photo, using the same cosine similarity.

decision.choice: OpenCLIP ViT-B-32 with the laion2b_s34b_b79k weights, run locally on CPU
decision.why: One model covers both photo-to-text and photo-to-photo. It is the example model in the OpenCLIP README, small enough for a laptop or a single office machine, and running locally means photos never leave the site.

alternatives.name: openai/clip-vit-base-patch32 via transformers
alternatives.tradeoff: The original OpenAI weights through Hugging Face; similar size, a different training set, so compare both on your eval.

alternatives.name: A larger model from open_clip.list_pretrained()
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick if the eval shows small models miss fine detail; costs more memory and slower embedding.

alternatives.name: Hosted multimodal embedding API
alternatives.tradeoff: No local compute, but every photo goes to a third party, which is hard to justify for personal belongings.

steps.delegate: Python, open_clip_torch, torch, Pillow. Write embed.py with load_model() returning (model, preprocess, tokenizer) for ViT-B-32 / laion2b_s34b_b79k in eval mode, embed_images(paths) and embed_texts(strings), both returning L2-normalized float32 numpy arrays. Tests: output norms are 1 within 1e-5; same input gives the same vector twice; a photo of a mug scores higher with 'a photo of a mug' than 'a photo of a bicycle'.
verify: Embedding 100 photos runs on your machine and you recorded seconds per image
Your mug vs bicycle sanity test passes on your own photos

steps.title: Score a found photo against text and photo reports
steps.learn: Image-to-text and image-to-image similarities live on different scales, so adding them raw lets one dominate. Short owner descriptions also differ from captions CLIP saw in training, so phrasing like 'a photo of a ...' around the description is something to test, not assume.

decision.choice: Score = image-to-text cosine; when an owner photo exists, combine with image-to-image cosine after per-type z-scoring
decision.why: Text is always present so it is the base score. Z-scoring each similarity type against the current candidate pool puts them on a common scale before combining, so an owner photo helps without swamping the text signal.

alternatives.name: Caption the found photo with a VLM, then match text to text
alternatives.tradeoff: Readable captions staff can check, but adds a slower model and its caption errors become matching errors.

alternatives.name: Max of the two raw cosines
alternatives.tradeoff: Simple, but the scales differ so the photo score usually wins whenever it exists.

steps.delegate: In match.py write score(found_vec, reports) where each report has a text vector and an optional photo vector. Compute cosines, z-score each type over the candidate pool, and combine with weight w (default 0.5) when a photo exists. Add a prompt_template option for text, e.g. 'a photo of {}'. Tests: identical image beats a random one; a report without a photo still gets a finite score; changing w changes ranks only for reports with photos.
verify: On your 30 labeled text reports, you compared Recall@5 with and without the prompt template
You can show one case where the owner photo moved the correct report up

steps.title: Apply date, zone and category filters before ranking
steps.learn: An item found before it was reported lost, or across campus, is rarely a match. Filtering first shrinks the pool and removes look-alikes. CLIP can also guess a coarse category for the found photo zero-shot by comparing it with prompts for each category name.

decision.choice: Hard filter on date (found within or after the lost window); soft boost for same zone and same zero-shot category
decision.why: Dates are reliable and wrong ones are near impossible matches, so they are safe to filter. Owners often misremember where, and zero-shot categories can be wrong, so those only adjust scores instead of hiding the true report.

alternatives.name: Filter on all fields
alternatives.tradeoff: Smallest pool and fastest, but one wrong zone or category guess hides the right report entirely.

alternatives.name: No filters, similarity only
alternatives.tradeoff: Never wrongly excludes, but look-alike items from other days and places crowd the top 5.

steps.delegate: Extend match.py: candidates(found_item) queries lost reports whose window allows the found date (with a configurable grace in days). Add zero_shot_category(found_vec, category_names) using CLIP text prompts. Apply additive boosts for zone and category matches. Tests: a report lost after the found date is excluded; zone mismatch lowers but does not remove; category list changes are picked up without code edits.
verify: Recall@5 on your labeled set with filters is at least as high as without them
You measured how often the zero-shot category is correct on your own photos

steps.title: Choose how to store and search the vectors
steps.learn: A campus or office lost-and-found holds hundreds to a few thousand open reports, and filtering shrinks that further. At that size an exact scan over a matrix of normalized vectors is fast, and exact search means misses are the model's fault, not the index's.

decision.choice: Exact search: keep vectors in a numpy matrix (persisted in SQLite as blobs) and score with one matrix product
decision.why: The pool is small after filters, so exact search costs little and has no recall loss to debug. It also keeps deployment to a single process with no separate vector service.

alternatives.name: FAISS IndexFlatIP
alternatives.tradeoff: Same exact result with a faster kernel; worth it once a city-wide system holds far more reports.

alternatives.name: HNSW (hnswlib or a vector DB)
alternatives.tradeoff: Pick for very large pools; adds approximate misses and index upkeep for a problem this size does not have.

steps.delegate: Write store.py: save and load float32 vectors as SQLite BLOBs keyed by record id; build_matrix(ids) returns an (n, d) numpy array. Score candidates with a single matrix product. Tests: round-trip preserves vectors exactly; scores equal per-row dot products; query over 5,000 vectors finishes under a timing budget you set and record.
verify: You recorded query latency over 5,000 synthetic reports on your target machine
Results match a per-row loop exactly on 100 random queries

steps.title: Evaluate matching offline on a public dataset
steps.learn: Photo-to-photo matching can be measured at scale on Stanford Online Products: use one image of a product as the found photo and another image of the same product as the owner's photo. Text matching is measured on your own labeled reports, since the dataset has no owner-style descriptions.

decision.choice: Simulate pools of 500 owner photos with one true match each, report Recall@1, Recall@5 and MRR
decision.why: A pool of hundreds matches the size of a real campus backlog better than searching all 120k images, so the numbers predict what staff would see.

alternatives.name: Retrieve over the whole dataset
alternatives.tradeoff: Standard for metric-learning papers, but far harder than a real lost-and-found pool and understates usefulness.

alternatives.name: Only your hand-collected photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Most realistic images, but too few to tell small differences from noise.

steps.delegate: Write eval.py: sample products with at least two images from the dataset, build pools of 500 with one positive, embed with embed.py, rank with match.score, and print Recall@1, Recall@5, MRR with bootstrap 95 percent intervals over 20 pools. A second mode runs the same metrics on a CSV of your labeled text reports. Fixed seed. Tests: a perfect scorer gets 1.0; a random scorer gets near 5/500 for Recall@5.
verify: You report Recall@5 and MRR with confidence intervals on both the public set and your text set
You kept 10 of your text reports untouched until the final run, to check you did not overfit prompts

steps.title: Handle duplicates, weak matches and no-match cases
steps.learn: The same item may be photographed twice, many items are never reported, and some top matches are weak. A matcher that always shows 5 suggestions wastes staff time on items nobody lost. Perceptual hashes catch re-uploads cheaply; a calibrated score threshold separates 'check these' from 'no likely match'.

decision.choice: Perceptual hash to flag duplicate found photos; show matches only above a threshold chosen from the eval set
decision.why: Duplicates are exact or near-exact images, which hashing detects without the model. A threshold on the raw image-to-text cosine (not the pool z-scored score, which is relative) picked for a target precision on labeled data gives a decision staff can trust.

alternatives.name: Always show the top 5
alternatives.tradeoff: Never hides a real match, but every unreported item still produces 5 false leads.

alternatives.name: Use CLIP similarity for duplicates
alternatives.tradeoff: Already computed, but two different black umbrellas look like duplicates too.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. On found-item upload compute a perceptual hash and flag existing items within a Hamming distance you configure. Add calibrate.py that sweeps thresholds on the labeled eval output and prints precision and recall per threshold; store the chosen value in config. Tests: re-saved JPEG of the same photo is flagged; a different object is not; below-threshold items return an explicit no_match status.
verify: You chose a threshold and wrote down its precision and recall on held-out data
Uploading the same photo twice is flagged as a duplicate

steps.title: Keep a human in the loop to confirm and return items
steps.learn: A match is a suggestion. Returning a wallet to the wrong person is worse than not returning it. Staff confirm a candidate, then the claimant proves ownership with a detail that was not visible in any shared photo or listing.

decision.choice: Staff-only review page; claimant must answer an ownership question before handover
decision.why: Photos and descriptions can be seen by anyone browsing, so they cannot prove ownership. A hidden detail checked in person blocks false claims, and staff confirmation catches model mistakes.

alternatives.name: Auto-email the top match
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest, but a wrong match sends a stranger to claim the item and leaks that it was found.

alternatives.name: Public gallery of found items
alternatives.tradeoff: Owners can self-search, but it invites false claims and exposes photos of personal belongings.

steps.delegate: FastAPI + Jinja templates. Staff page lists a found item with its ranked candidate reports and scores; actions: confirm match, reject, mark returned. Store every action in an audit table with staff id and time. Notifications go only after confirmation. Tests: no notification without a confirm action; non-staff requests get 403; audit row written for each action.
verify: A teammate acting as staff can confirm a match in under a minute from the review page
The audit log shows who confirmed each return and when

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The app matches things, not people. Found photos can include bystanders' faces, and ID cards, phones and letters show personal data. Blur faces before anything is stored, and do not embed photos of documents (CLIP vectors can encode visible text); keep contact data out of the matcher.

decision.choice: Run on-device face detection on upload, blur faces before saving, discard the original
decision.why: If the original is never stored, a later leak or misuse cannot expose bystanders. Blurring before embedding also keeps faces out of the vectors, so the matcher cannot become a face search.

alternatives.name: Ask staff to crop photos manually
alternatives.tradeoff: No extra model, but people forget under time pressure and one missed face is a privacy leak.

projects.question: Can CLIP embeddings turn everyday walk photos into a collectible dex where sets are assigned by text prompts and rarity reflects how few similar finds exist?

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the test data
steps.learn: The game is two ML calls wrapped in a product: zero-shot set assignment (image vs text prompts) and rarity (how crowded the embedding neighborhood is). Success comes from the try-it: 10 friends play for a week, and you track what gets collected, how often players accept the set, and duplicates.

decision.choice: Offline check on COCO 2017 val images mapped to your sets, then a 10-friend, 7-day live test
decision.why: COCO gives labeled everyday objects for free, so you can measure set-assignment accuracy before anyone plays. The live week then measures what COCO cannot: real walk photos, duplicates, rarity drift and cheating.

alternatives.name: Live test only
alternatives.tradeoff: Fastest to start, but you cannot tell model errors from bad set design, and you burn your friends' patience debugging thresholds.

alternatives.name: Hand-label 300 of your own walk photos
alternatives.tradeoff: Closest to real use and worth doing later, but slower to build and biased toward what you happen to photograph.

verify: Write the one question and 3 metrics: set acceptance rate, duplicates missed per 100 captures, captures per player per day
Pick 10 to 20 sets and map at least 5 of them to COCO categories for the offline check

steps.title: Define collectible sets as text prompts for zero-shot sorting
steps.learn: CLIP maps images and text into one space, so a set like 'mailboxes' is just the embedding of prompts such as 'a photo of a mailbox.'. Averaging several templates per set (prompt ensembling, as in the CLIP repo notebook) makes the set vector less sensitive to wording.

decision.choice: open_clip ViT-B-32 (laion2b_s34b_b79k), 3 to 5 prompt templates per set, averaged and L2-normalized
decision.why: No labeled data is needed, so you can add a new set (say 'street murals') by writing text. ViT-B-32 is small enough to run on a cheap server or laptop for 10 players, and open_clip lists many alternative checkpoints if accuracy is too low.

alternatives.name: Fine-tuned image classifier
alternatives.tradeoff: Higher accuracy on fixed sets, but needs labeled photos per set and retraining every time you add a set.

alternatives.name: VLM caption, then map text to sets
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles odd objects and explains itself, but is slower and costlier per capture and its free text still needs mapping.

alternatives.name: Larger CLIP model (ViT-L)
alternatives.tradeoff: Usually better zero-shot accuracy, but more memory and latency per capture; worth it only if the offline check shows B-32 is the bottleneck.

steps.delegate: Python 3.11, open_clip, torch, Pillow. Write sets.yaml (set_id, display name, 3-5 prompt templates). Implement build_set_matrix(sets) returning normalized averaged text embeddings, and embed_image(path) returning a normalized vector. Add a CLI that ranks sets for an image. Tests: vectors have unit norm, set order is stable, a known COCO image of a dog ranks a 'dogs' set first.
verify: Run the CLI on 20 COCO val images from mapped categories and record top-1 accuracy
Compare one template vs averaged templates on the same 20 images and note the difference

steps.title: Add an 'unsorted' bucket with a similarity and margin threshold
steps.learn: Zero-shot always returns some top set, even for a photo of your shoe. Real walks are mostly things outside your sets, so the system must be able to say 'not a collectible'. Cosine similarity values are not calibrated probabilities, so thresholds must be tuned on data, not guessed.

decision.choice: Assign only if top-1 similarity is above a floor AND beats top-2 by a margin; otherwise 'unsorted'
decision.why: A floor rejects off-topic photos and a margin rejects photos that sit between two sets (fire hydrant vs bollard). Both are tuned on the COCO check plus a few dozen of your own off-topic photos, which keeps wrong awards rare, the failure players notice most.

alternatives.name: Softmax over sets with a probability cutoff
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to explain, but softmax over a small closed set can be confident on photos that match no set at all.

alternatives.name: Always assign top-1
alternatives.tradeoff: Maximizes collecting, but wrong sets erode trust fast in a game about getting the right thing.

alternatives.name: Add explicit negative prompts
alternatives.tradeoff: A 'background' or 'random object' set can absorb junk, but its behavior depends heavily on the wording you pick.

steps.delegate: Extend the Python module: assign(image_vec, set_matrix, floor, margin) returns set_id or 'unsorted' plus scores. Write tune_thresholds.py that grid-searches floor and margin on a labeled CSV (path, true_set or 'none') and prints precision of awarded sets and coverage. Tests: an all-equal score vector returns 'unsorted'; floor -1 and margin 0 reproduce plain top-1 except exact ties.
verify: Label 50 of your own off-topic walk photos as 'none' and include them in tuning
Pick thresholds and record precision of awarded sets and the fraction left unsorted

steps.title: Store image embeddings for neighbor queries
steps.learn: Rarity and dedup both ask 'which past captures are near this one?'. With 10 players for a week you have thousands of vectors at most, so exact search is cheap; the real design question is keeping vectors, users and captures consistent in one place.

decision.choice: Postgres with pgvector: one captures table holding user, set, location, time and the vector
decision.why: One database means a capture, its vector and its rarity commit together, and SQL filters (same set, same user, last 24 hours) sit next to pgvector's cosine distance operator. Exact scans are fine at this scale; pgvector also offers HNSW if the game grows.

alternatives.name: FAISS in memory (IndexFlatIP)
alternatives.tradeoff: Very fast exact search, but you must persist and rebuild it yourself and keep it in sync with the database.

alternatives.name: NumPy brute force over a saved array
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest code for a prototype, but concurrency, filtering and persistence become your problem.

alternatives.name: Managed vector database
alternatives.tradeoff: Scales and handles indexing, but adds a second system and cost for a dataset that fits in one table.

steps.delegate: Docker Compose with Postgres plus the pgvector extension. Python with psycopg and pgvector. Functions: insert_capture, neighbors(vec, set_id, k), count_within(vec, set_id, max_cosine_distance). Tests: neighbors of a stored vector returns itself first; set_id filter excludes other sets.
verify: Insert 1,000 COCO embeddings and time neighbors() and count_within(); record p50 latency
Check that the embedding dimension in the schema matches the model output

steps.title: Compute rarity from nearest-neighbor counts
steps.learn: Rarity is a density estimate: few captures within a radius means rare. With few items, density estimates are very noisy: on day one everything looks legendary, and one player photographing the same street can make a set look common. Decide whether rarity is frozen at capture time or recomputed.

decision.choice: Same-set neighbor count within a cosine radius, over captures plus a seed corpus; quantile tiers, frozen at award
decision.why: A seed corpus (COCO embeddings per set) acts as a prior so early finds are not all legendary. Counting within a radius is easy to explain to players, quantile tiers keep the tier mix stable as data grows, and freezing avoids taking rewards away.

alternatives.name: Distance to the k-th nearest neighbor
alternatives.tradeoff: No radius to tune and adapts to scale, but very noisy when a set has fewer than k items.

alternatives.name: Kernel density estimate
alternatives.tradeoff: Smoother scores (sklearn KernelDensity), but the bandwidth choice drives everything and is hard to set with little data.

alternatives.name: Rarity by set frequency only
alternatives.tradeoff: Stable and simple, but every mailbox gets the same rarity, ignoring that a blue antique one is unusual.

steps.delegate: Python module rarity.py: rarity_score(vec, set_id) using count_within over captures and seed vectors with per-source weights; tiers from quantiles recomputed nightly and stored in a tiers table. Store awarded tier on the capture row. Tests: with an empty set the seed corpus gives a non-legendary tier for a typical image; adding 20 near-identical vectors lowers the next one's tier.
verify: Simulate a week: replay COCO images in random order and plot tier counts per day
Show 5 'legendary' and 5 'common' results to a friend and record whether they agree

steps.title: Stop the same object being collected twice
steps.learn: Two kinds of duplicate: the same photo re-uploaded (pixel-level near duplicate) and the same physical object shot again from another angle. Perceptual hashes catch the first; embeddings plus place and time catch the second. Two different but identical-looking mailboxes are the hard case.

decision.choice: Per player: pHash Hamming check, then same set + high CLIP similarity + within a small distance of a past capture
decision.why: pHash (imagehash, Hamming distance via hash subtraction) is cheap and robust to resizing and re-encoding, so it catches re-uploads. Requiring location proximity before calling a CLIP match a duplicate avoids blocking two different mailboxes in different streets, which similarity alone cannot tell apart.

alternatives.name: pHash only
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap, but misses the same object photographed from a new angle or distance.

alternatives.name: CLIP similarity only
alternatives.tradeoff: Catches new angles, but merges distinct look-alike objects, blocking honest captures.

alternatives.name: Keypoint matching (ORB or SIFT)
alternatives.tradeoff: Better at 'same physical instance', but heavier per pair and fragile across lighting and season.

steps.delegate: Python, imagehash, Pillow. Implement is_duplicate(user_id, image, vec, lat, lon) returning (bool, reason). Steps: phash Hamming distance against the player's captures; then pgvector query for same set within a cosine threshold and haversine distance under N meters. Tests: identical file is duplicate; a resized copy is duplicate; same object 2 km away is not.
verify: Photograph 5 objects twice from different angles and confirm all 5 second shots are flagged
Photograph 2 look-alike objects in different places and confirm neither is flagged

steps.title: Build a simple multi-user backend for captures and dexes
steps.learn: The backend owns identity, the capture pipeline (embed, assign, dedup, rarity, store) and each player's dex. For 10 friends the main risks are not scale but correctness: two uploads racing, a slow model call blocking requests, and partial writes.

decision.choice: FastAPI service with server-side embedding, one model loaded at startup, Postgres transaction per capture
decision.why: Server-side embedding keeps one model version for everyone so rarity is comparable across players. Postgres's default READ COMMITTED lets two concurrent transactions both pass the dedup check, so take a per-user advisory lock before checking. 10 players do not need queues; load the model once.

alternatives.name: On-device embedding
alternatives.tradeoff: Better privacy and offline play, but needs a mobile-sized model and every client must run the same version.

alternatives.name: Job queue with workers
alternatives.tradeoff: Smooths bursts and retries, but adds moving parts you do not need at 10 users.

alternatives.name: Backend-as-a-service (auth plus database)
alternatives.tradeoff: Faster auth and storage, but you still need a server process to run the model.

steps.delegate: Python FastAPI app. Endpoints: POST /captures (multipart image plus lat, lon, nonce) returns {set, tier, duplicate, reason}; GET /dex/{user_id}; GET /leaderboard. Token auth per player. Load open_clip once at startup. In one transaction, take pg_advisory_xact_lock(user_id), then run the dedup check and insert. Tests with pytest and httpx: two concurrent identical uploads yield one award; unsorted images are stored but not awarded.
verify: Upload 50 photos from two phones at once and confirm no double awards
Record p50 and p95 upload-to-result latency on your server

steps.title: Add anti-cheat basics
steps.learn: Players will photograph screens, upload web images, share photos between accounts and spoof GPS. You cannot stop a determined cheater, so aim to make cheating harder than playing and to detect the cheap tricks.

decision.choice: In-app camera only, server nonce, cross-player pHash, rate limits, and a 'photo of a screen' prompt check
decision.why: A short-lived, single-use nonce blocks replayed requests; camera-only capture is enforced only by your client, so it stops casual gallery uploads but not a modified client. Cross-player pHash catches shared photos. A zero-shot 'photo of a screen' check flags rephotographed images for review, not auto-bans.

alternatives.name: Platform attestation (Play Integrity, App Attest)
alternatives.tradeoff: Proves a genuine app on a genuine device, but requires native apps and store setup that a friends test may not justify.

alternatives.name: Trust the client
alternatives.tradeoff: Fine among close friends, but rarity data gets polluted by any cheating and you cannot tell later.

alternatives.name: Manual moderation of rare finds
alternatives.tradeoff: Accurate for the few legendary awards, but does not scale and delays rewards.

steps.delegate: Extend the FastAPI app: GET /nonce issues a signed, 2-minute nonce bound to the user; POST /captures rejects missing, reused or expired nonces. Add per-user rate limit (captures per minute). Add cross-user pHash lookup and a screen-photo score using open_clip prompts; flag, do not reject. Tests: reused nonce is rejected; 11th capture in a minute is throttled; same image from two users is flagged.
verify: Try 3 cheats yourself (screen photo, shared image, replayed request) and record which are caught
Check flagged captures land in a review list, not silently awarded

steps.title: Handle failures and model upgrades without breaking the dex
steps.learn: Embeddings from different models live in different spaces, so mixing them silently breaks rarity and dedup. Thresholds (set floor and margin, dedup cosine, rarity radius, tier quantiles) are model-specific too and must be retuned. Plan for model swaps, failed uploads and retries from day one.

decision.choice: Store model_id with every vector, re-embed everything on upgrade, keep awarded tiers frozen; idempotent upload key
decision.why: Re-embedding a week of photos is cheap at this scale and keeps one consistent space. Freezing awards means an upgrade never takes a prize away. An idempotency key on uploads makes phone retries on bad signal safe.

alternatives.name: Never upgrade the model
alternatives.tradeoff: Zero migration work, but you are stuck with early mistakes in set assignment.

alternatives.name: Keep old and new vectors side by side
alternatives.tradeoff: No downtime during migration, but every query must pick the right space and storage doubles.

steps.delegate: Add model_id to captures and seed vectors; write reembed.py that streams stored images, writes new vectors under the new model_id, then switches an active_model setting. Add Idempotency-Key header handling to POST /captures. Tests: queries never mix model_ids; a retried request with the same key returns the original result without a second insert.
verify: Switch to a second open_clip checkpoint on a copy of the data and confirm queries only use the active model_id
Kill the server mid-upload and confirm the retry produces exactly one capture

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Collect things, places, plants and animals, never people. Walk photos will include passers-by, faces, house numbers and precise home locations. Also, a game that rewards rare finds can push people onto private property or toward touching wild plants and animals.

decision.choice: On-device face check rejects or blurs before upload; no 'person' sets; coarsen stored location; safety rules in-app
decision.why: Running a face detector (for example MediaPipe Face Detector) on the phone means faces never reach the server, so they are never stored. Coarse location still supports dedup without logging where each player lives.

alternatives.name: Server-side face blurring
alternatives.tradeoff: Simpler client, but raw faces reach your server even if only briefly.

alternatives.name: No face handling
alternatives.tradeoff: Least work, but you would store bystanders' faces without consent.

steps.delegate: Add an on-device step using MediaPipe Face Detector with the BlazeFace full-range model (rear-camera photos; short-range targets selfie distance): if any face is detected, block the capture with a message, or blur boxes before upload. Server: round lat and lon to about 100 m precision before storing, strip EXIF. Tests: an image with a face never reaches the upload endpoint; stored rows contain no full-precision coordinates.

Confirm no set prompt targets people, and the app says not to enter private land or handle wildlife

steps.learn: The try-it is the real evaluation: play with 10 friends for a week and track what gets collected. Log every capture with its scores so you can replay decisions later, and give players a one-tap 'wrong set' button so you get labels for free.

steps.title: Frame the question, the success metric and the data
steps.learn: Prices for the same item vary across stores and weeks. The answer only holds if three things work: reading receipts correctly, knowing two lines are the same product, and comparing per unit. Success: after a month, a per-item cheapest-store table you trust, with error rates for each stage.

decision.choice: Your own month of receipts as main data; CORD v2 to test OCR and parsing; Open Prices as a price reference
decision.why: Only your receipts answer your question. CORD v2 (labeled receipts, CC BY 4.0) lets you measure parsing before you have many receipts, though its receipts are Indonesian shop and restaurant receipts, not your stores. Open Prices is an open crowdsourced price dataset (ODbL) to sanity-check prices.

alternatives.name: SROIE (ICDAR 2019) receipts
alternatives.tradeoff: A standard receipt OCR and key-field benchmark, but it labels totals and header fields rather than individual line items.

steps.title: Capture receipts so OCR has a fair chance
steps.learn: Most OCR errors start at capture: thermal paper fades, receipts curl, long receipts do not fit one frame, and shadows break binarization. Some stores also offer digital receipts, which skip OCR entirely.

decision.choice: Phone photo with page detection and perspective correction, plus import of digital receipts where available
decision.why: Photos work for every store, and flattening the receipt before OCR fixes skew and curl cheaply. Digital receipts (email or store app) are exact text, so they are a free accuracy win and a ground truth for checking your OCR on the same store's layout.

alternatives.name: Flatbed scanner
alternatives.tradeoff: Best image quality and consistent resolution, but too much friction to keep up for a month.

alternatives.name: Digital receipts only
alternatives.tradeoff: No OCR errors at all, but most stores or payment paths do not provide them, so coverage is partial.

steps.title: Choose the OCR engine
steps.learn: OCR returns text plus boxes; receipts are hard because of narrow fonts, faded print and columns of prices. Tesseract's docs advise at least 300 DPI, note its built-in Otsu binarization struggles with uneven backgrounds, and say to pick a page segmentation mode (--psm). Measure engines on your receipts.

decision.choice: Local OCR with line boxes (PaddleOCR, or Apple Vision text recognition on iOS), with Tesseract as the baseline
decision.why: Local engines keep receipts off third-party servers and cost nothing per page. Line-level boxes let the parser align item names with prices. Running Tesseract with tuned --psm as a baseline tells you whether the heavier engine is worth it.

alternatives.name: AWS Textract AnalyzeExpense
alternatives.tradeoff: Receipt-aware cloud API that returns line items and fields, but costs per page and sends receipts to a third party.

alternatives.name: VLM reads the image to JSON
alternatives.tradeoff: Handles messy layouts with no parser, but may produce plausible wrong prices; needs checks against the receipt total.

alternatives.name: Donut (OCR-free model)
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns image to structured output end to end, but needs fine-tuning on receipts like yours to beat a tuned pipeline.

steps.title: Parse line items, quantities, discounts and totals
steps.learn: A receipt line is not always an item: there are quantity lines ('2 @ 1.99'), weighed items ('1.32 lb @ 2.49/lb'), coupon lines that belong to the item above, tax flags and subtotals. The receipt total is a free check: items minus discounts should equal the subtotal.

decision.choice: Rule-based parser with per-store patterns, validated by a subtotal checksum; LLM extraction only when the checksum fails
decision.why: Each store's layout repeats, so a few regexes per store are cheap, fast and explainable. The checksum catches OCR and parsing errors automatically. An LLM with a strict JSON schema (for example Pydantic) is a fallback, and its output must pass the same checksum.

alternatives.name: LLM extraction for every receipt
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on unseen layouts with no rules, but costs per receipt and can invent or drop lines.

alternatives.name: Train a layout model on CORD
alternatives.tradeoff: Learns structure from labels, but CORD's layouts differ from your stores, so you would need your own labels.

steps.title: Normalize sizes and compute unit prices
steps.learn: '2% milk 1gal' and 'Milk 2% 128oz' are the same size: a US gallon is 128 US fluid ounces. Comparing sticker prices across sizes is unfair, so convert to a base unit (ml, g or count) and compare price per unit. Watch for 'oz' meaning weight vs fluid ounces, and sizes missing from the receipt.

decision.choice: Parse size strings to quantities with pint, convert to ml, g or count; fill missing sizes from the product record
decision.why: A units library (pint's UnitRegistry) handles conversions and refuses invalid ones like mass to volume, which catches parsing bugs. Receipts often abbreviate or omit size, so the canonical product (or an Open Food Facts quantity) supplies it.

alternatives.name: Hand-written conversion table
alternatives.tradeoff: No dependency and easy to read, but every new unit and abbreviation is a manual edit and errors are silent.

Confirm 1 gal and 128 fl oz give the same unit price for the same price

steps.title: Define what 'the same item' means and build the catalog
steps.learn: Before matching, decide the comparison level: the exact product (one brand, one size) or a comparable class (any brand of 2% milk, compared per unit). Receipts use store abbreviations ('MLK 2PCT GAL'), so you need a canonical product table plus an alias table per store.

decision.choice: Canonical comparable-product classes (category, attributes, base unit) with per-store alias rows
decision.why: Different stores sell different brands, so exact-product matching would leave few items comparable across stores. A class like 'milk, 2%, per liter' answers your actual question. Aliases learned once per store make later receipts match instantly.

alternatives.name: Exact product by barcode (UPC/EAN)
alternatives.tradeoff: Precise and unambiguous, but receipts usually show store codes or abbreviations, not barcodes.

alternatives.name: Free-form text, no catalog
alternatives.tradeoff: No upfront work, but every comparison needs fresh matching and results drift.

steps.delegate: SQLite schema: products(id, name, category, attributes JSON, base_unit), aliases(store_id, raw_text_normalized, product_id, source in [rule, fuzzy, embedding, llm, human], confidence). Normalizer: lowercase, expand a per-store abbreviation dictionary (YAML), strip sizes and prices. Seed with your 20 most-bought items. Tests: normalizer is idempotent; same raw text at the same store maps to the same product.
verify: Write the class definition for your 20 most-bought items and get the list reviewed by one other person
Record how many receipt lines in week one map via exact alias

steps.title: Match receipt lines to products: rules, fuzzy, embeddings, LLM
steps.learn: Use the cheapest method that is confident, then escalate. Fuzzy string scores handle reordering and typos; embeddings handle synonyms; an LLM handles cryptic abbreviations. Each needs a threshold, and a wrong match is worse than no match because it corrupts price comparisons.

decision.choice: Cascade: alias, RapidFuzz token_set_ratio, sentence-transformers top-k, LLM pick; low confidence to review
decision.why: Most lines repeat, so aliases and fuzzy matching resolve them at near zero cost. Embeddings shortlist candidates for the rest, and the LLM only chooses among that shortlist. Confirmed matches become aliases, so the expensive steps shrink each week.

alternatives.name: LLM for every line
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest pipeline, but costs per line, adds latency and may match the same text differently on different days.

alternatives.name: Fuzzy matching only
alternatives.tradeoff: Free and fast, but fails on abbreviations that share few characters with the product name.

alternatives.name: Manual matching
alternatives.tradeoff: Perfectly accurate for one person, but tedious enough that you stop after week two.

steps.delegate: Python, rapidfuzz, sentence-transformers. match(raw, store_id) returns (product_id or None, method, score). Stages with configurable thresholds; block candidates by category and unit dimension; LLM gets raw text plus top-5 candidates and must answer an id or 'none'. Cache LLM answers as aliases with source='llm'. Tests: alias hit skips later stages; an incompatible unit dimension is never matched.
verify: Label 100 receipt lines by hand and record precision and coverage per stage
Record how many LLM calls were needed in week 1 vs week 4

steps.title: Store price history you can reprocess
steps.learn: Each matched line becomes a price observation: product, store, date, unit price, whether it was on promotion. Parsers and matchers will improve, so keep raw OCR and parse output and record which version produced each observation, so history can be rebuilt instead of hand-fixed.

decision.choice: SQLite with receipts, raw_lines, observations tables; observations derived and versioned, raw data immutable
decision.why: One person's month of receipts is small, and a single file is easy to back up and query. Keeping raw data immutable and observations derived means a matcher fix is a re-run, not a manual edit. Use transactions so a receipt's observations commit together.

alternatives.name: Postgres
alternatives.tradeoff: Better for many users and concurrent writers, but more setup than one person needs.

alternatives.name: Spreadsheet
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy to eyeball and edit, but no reprocessing, weak typing and easy to corrupt.

steps.delegate: Python, sqlite3. Tables: stores, receipts(id, store_id, date, image_path), raw_lines(receipt_id, ocr_engine, text, bbox), observations(product_id, store_id, date, unit_price, regular_or_promo, pipeline_version). rebuild_observations(version) re-derives from raw_lines in one transaction. Tests: rebuild is idempotent; deleting a receipt removes its observations; dates parse to ISO.
verify: Change one alias and rebuild; confirm only the affected observations change
Query the unit price history of one item across all stores

steps.title: Compare stores fairly
steps.learn: 'Cheapest' is easy to get wrong: one promotion can win the month, prices move week to week, and an item seen once at a store is not evidence. Separate regular from promotional prices, align by week, require a minimum number of observations, and report coverage alongside the answer.

decision.choice: Per item: median regular unit price per store, items seen at 2+ stores with min observations, promos apart
decision.why: The median resists one-off sales and OCR outliers. Requiring the same item at two or more stores means each comparison is real. Showing promo prices separately answers 'where is it cheap on sale' without hiding the everyday price.

alternatives.name: Lowest price ever seen
alternatives.tradeoff: Easy and exciting, but rewards one-time promotions you may never see again.

alternatives.name: Basket index across stores
alternatives.tradeoff: Answers 'which store overall', but hides per-item differences and needs the same basket at every store.

steps.delegate: Python, pandas. compare(month) returns per product: store, median_regular_unit_price, n_obs, min_promo_price, and a winner only when n_obs meets a threshold at 2+ stores. Output a CSV and a short text table. Tests: a single promo observation cannot make a store the winner; items seen at one store are listed as 'not comparable'.
verify: Report how many of your 20 top items had a valid comparison
For 3 winners, check a shelf price in person and record whether the ranking held

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: Receipts identify things and places, but also people: partial card numbers, loyalty IDs, cashier names, and a timestamped log of where you shop. Keep products and stores, drop the rest. Prices are a helper from your past receipts, and shelf prices and store terms are the official source.

decision.choice: Redact payment, loyalty and cashier lines at parse time; keep images local; cloud OCR or LLM only with explicit opt-in
decision.why: The question needs product, store, date and price only. Dropping identifying lines before storage removes most risk, and keeping images local means no cloud service sees anything unless you opt in; Textract opt-in uploads the whole image, so crop off payment lines first.

alternatives.name: Store everything, secure the database
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps full detail for debugging, but any leak exposes payment and shopping-pattern data.

alternatives.name: Delete images after parsing
alternatives.tradeoff: Smallest footprint, but you lose the ability to re-run better OCR later.

steps.delegate: Python. Add redact(lines) before storage: drop lines matching card patterns (masked digits, 'VISA', 'AUTH'), loyalty or member numbers, and cashier name lines per store config. Add a config flag allow_cloud=false that blocks Textract and LLM calls. Tests: fixtures with card and loyalty lines produce no stored digits; with allow_cloud=false no network call is made.
verify: Grep the database for 4-digit card fragments and loyalty numbers and confirm none remain
Confirm the app labels prices as 'from your receipts on DATE' and says to check the shelf

steps.title: Test it outside: a month of real receipts
steps.learn: The try-it: scan every receipt for a month and find the cheapest store per item. Measure each stage so you know which one limits the answer, and log manual fixes as labels.
verify: Report receipts scanned, share passing the checksum, and line-item recall on 10 hand-checked receipts
Report match precision on 100 labeled lines and the share needing review
Produce the cheapest-store table with n_obs per cell and the share of items comparable
Record minutes per week spent on manual fixes

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: The 4-part write-up: (1) the one question, (2) numbers for every claim with the machine and command, (3) why the surprising results happened (for example a store winning only through promos, or a matcher error), (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: Part 1 states the one question in one sentence
Part 2 gives OCR, parsing, matching and comparison numbers, each with machine and command
Part 3 explains at least 2 surprising results with evidence
Part 4 lists assumptions (one shopper, one month, your stores) and what this does not prove

projects.question: Which bird species visit my feeder, and at what times of day and season, measured by a camera that classifies on the device?

steps.title: Frame the question, the metric and the setup
steps.learn: The output is visit events (species, time, confidence), charted by hour and week across a season. Two numbers make it credible: classifier accuracy on your own labeled captures, and the false-trigger rate. Google's birds model card says it is not for counting or population statistics, so report visits, not populations.

decision.choice: Raspberry Pi camera with Picamera2, a pretrained bird classifier, and your own labeled captures as the test set
decision.why: Picamera2 gives Python access to frames plus a low-res stream for cheap motion checks, and pretrained iNaturalist bird models exist in TFLite form. Your own captures are the only honest test: lighting, angle and local species differ from public photos.

alternatives.name: Evaluate only on NABirds or CUB-200-2011
alternatives.tradeoff: Public, labeled and easy, but curated photos look nothing like a feeder cam; CUB also warns its images overlap ImageNet, which can inflate scores.

alternatives.name: Buy a commercial smart feeder
alternatives.tradeoff: Works on day one, but you cannot see or measure the model, the trigger or the data, so you cannot answer the question yourself.

verify: Write the question, the visit-event definition and the two credibility metrics in one paragraph
List 10 to 20 species you expect locally (from eBird data for your area) to compare against the model's label list
Confirm each expected species appears in the classifier's label file, and note those that do not

steps.title: Choose the board, camera and mounting
steps.learn: The bird model card says it suits a well-cropped image of a bird, so framing matters more than megapixels: a fixed perch at a fixed distance, plain background, no direct sun into the lens. The board must run a small detector and classifier at a few frames per second.

decision.choice: A Raspberry Pi 4 or 5 with a Raspberry Pi camera module, in a weatherproof box aimed at one perch
decision.why: It runs Linux, Python, Picamera2 and LiteRT out of the box, so you can iterate on the pipeline in hours. The Picamera2 manual documents lores streams and circular buffers that this project needs for triggering.

alternatives.name: ESP32 camera board (ESP-WHO, ESP-DL)
alternatives.tradeoff: Cheap and low power, suited to battery, but tight memory and C toolchains; you may only fit trigger plus tiny model and push images elsewhere.

alternatives.name: Raspberry Pi AI Camera (IMX500)
alternatives.tradeoff: Runs the network on the sensor, freeing the CPU, but models must be packaged as RPK files with Sony's tools, which adds a conversion step.

steps.delegate: Write a Python script for Raspberry Pi OS using Picamera2 that captures a still every 10 s for one hour, saves timestamped JPEGs, and logs vcgencmd measure_temp output. Add a mounting-check mode that overlays a target box where the perch should appear. Use a venv created with --system-site-packages (libcamera bindings are not on PyPI).
verify: From a 1-hour test, confirm a bird on the perch fills a sizable part of the frame (measure box width in pixels)
Check images at morning, noon and evening for glare or backlight and adjust the angle
Log SoC temperature inside the closed box on a sunny day; the Pi throttles from 80 C, so stay well below

steps.title: Trigger on motion and keep a pre-roll buffer
steps.learn: Running the model on every frame wastes power. Picamera2's example compares consecutive greyscale frames from a 320x240 lores stream by mean squared error and starts recording past a threshold; CircularOutput keeps seconds of video from before the trigger so the arrival is not lost.

decision.choice: Frame differencing on the lores stream inside a region-of-interest mask around the perch, plus a pre-roll buffer
decision.why: It costs almost nothing per frame, needs no extra hardware, and the mask ignores swaying branches and the street. The pre-roll means the classifier gets frames from the moment the bird lands.

alternatives.name: PIR motion sensor
alternatives.tradeoff: Very low power and lets the board sleep, but it senses heat changes, not pixels; test whether it fires for small birds at your distance.

alternatives.name: Run the detector at a fixed rate (e.g. 1 fps)
alternatives.tradeoff: No tuning of thresholds and catches still birds, but uses far more CPU and energy all day.

steps.delegate: Extend the Picamera2 script: main 1280x720 RGB888 and lores 320x240 YUV420; compute MSE on the Y plane inside a configurable ROI mask, casting to int16 before subtracting (uint8 wraps); on trigger, save a burst of N main frames and a short clip via CircularOutput2 (or CircularOutput); debounce with a cooldown. Log every trigger with its MSE. Unit test the ROI MSE on synthetic arrays, including darker-than-before frames.
verify: On a windy day, count triggers per hour with no bird present and tune the threshold and ROI to cut them
Review one hour of continuous stills and count birds that never triggered (miss rate)
Confirm the saved burst includes the frame where the bird lands (pre-roll works)

steps.title: Detect the bird, crop it, then classify the species
steps.learn: A detector finds a bird box; a fine-grained classifier names the species from the crop. Coral lists a quantized MobileNet V2 trained on iNaturalist 2017 for 900+ birds at 224x224, with CPU and Edge TPU builds. COCO-trained detectors include a bird class. Keep top-3 scores, not just top-1.

decision.choice: Two stages: COCO SSD detector (bird class) on lores, then the iNat bird MobileNet V2 on a main-frame crop
decision.why: The classifier expects a well-cropped bird, and crops from the high-res stream keep detail on small birds. The detector also rejects false triggers (leaves, squirrels) before the classifier, and its person class is what the privacy step uses.

alternatives.name: Classifier only on the whole frame
alternatives.tradeoff: Half the compute and simpler, but birds small in frame get misread, and you lose the person and no-bird filter.

alternatives.name: Fine-tune your own classifier on local species
alternatives.tradeoff: Fewer, local classes usually help, but you need hundreds of labeled crops first; plan it after a few weeks of data.

steps.delegate: In Python with ai_edge_litert.interpreter.Interpreter, load a COCO SSD MobileNet TFLite model and the Coral iNat bird TFLite classifier (CPU build) with its label file. Pipeline: detect on lores, keep boxes labeled bird above a score, map to main-frame coordinates, pad 10%, crop, resize to 224, classify, return top-3. Tests: fixed sample images give stable outputs, uint8 vs float input handled from input_details, timings per stage logged.
verify: On 50 saved triggers, check by eye that boxes cover the bird and crops are not clipped
Measure per-stage latency on the device (median of 100 runs) and write it down
Confirm triggers with no bird produce no classification event

steps.title: Decide model size and what runs on device vs laptop
steps.learn: LiteRT post-training quantization: dynamic range (weights only, no calibration data), full integer (needs a representative dataset; CPU, Edge TPU, microcontrollers) and float16. Distillation (Hinton et al.) trains a small student to match a large teacher's outputs, which you can do with your own unlabeled captures.

decision.choice: Device: trigger, int8 models, logging. Laptop: re-label crops with a larger model, train students
decision.why: The feeder must work when the Wi-Fi is down, so every visit gets a label on the device. The laptop has time and compute to re-label low-confidence events and, after a few weeks, distill a smaller local-species student that runs back on the Pi.

alternatives.name: Stream everything to the laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Any model size, no device tuning, but needs reliable Wi-Fi and the laptop on all season; one outage loses data.

alternatives.name: Everything on device, never reprocess
alternatives.tradeoff: Simplest, but errors are frozen in; you cannot improve old events when you get a better model.

alternatives.name: Zero-shot CLIP teacher on the laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Labels species by text prompt with no training, useful as a teacher, but accuracy on fine-grained birds must be checked on your labels.

steps.delegate: Write a laptop-side Python tool: load saved crops, run a larger teacher (a float classifier or CLIP via open_clip) to get soft labels, train a MobileNetV2 student on local species with a distillation loss, convert with tf.lite.TFLiteConverter using full integer quantization and a representative dataset of 200 crops, and compare student vs teacher accuracy on a held-out labeled set.
verify: After labeling in the accuracy step, compare float vs int8 classifier accuracy on the same 200 labeled crops and report the drop
Compare int8 latency on the Pi against float latency on the Pi
Unplug Wi-Fi for an hour and confirm events are still labeled and logged on the device
