steps.title: Turn detections into visit events and log them
steps.learn: A chickadee on the perch for 20 seconds yields many detections but one visit. Group consecutive detections into a visit until no bird is seen for a gap, and store one row per visit with time span, species votes and model version. Store UTC timestamps; convert only for charts.

decision.choice: SQLite on the device in WAL mode, one visits table plus a detections table, crops saved as files referenced by path
decision.why: SQLite is a single file with transactions, so a power cut mid-write does not corrupt the log, and WAL mode lets the sync reader run while the camera loop writes. It is queryable for charts with no server.

alternatives.name: Append-only JSON Lines files
alternatives.tradeoff: Trivial and easy to ship, but partial lines after a power loss and no queries without loading everything.

alternatives.name: A time-series database
alternatives.tradeoff: Good for dashboards, but a server process on a small board and overkill for a few hundred rows a day.

steps.delegate: In Python, write a visit aggregator: input detection stream (ts, top-3 species and scores, box, crop path); a visit ends after G seconds with no bird; species is the score-weighted vote across detections. Store visits(uuid, start_utc, end_utc, species, conf, top3_json, model_version, synced) and detections in SQLite with journal_mode=WAL. Tests: synthetic streams with gaps, two birds overlapping, crash mid-visit recovery.
verify: Watch 20 real visits live and confirm each produced exactly one visit row
Pull the power during a visit, reboot, and confirm the database opens and earlier rows are intact
Confirm timestamps are UTC and the board clock was synced (record how you checked)

steps.title: Sync events over flaky Wi-Fi without losing or duplicating
steps.learn: Outdoor Wi-Fi drops. Treat the device as the source of truth: mark rows unsynced, upload in batches, and mark synced only after the receiver confirms. Because each visit has a UUID, the receiver can upsert, so a retried batch after a timeout creates no duplicates.

decision.choice: An outbox: periodic batch upload of unsynced visits keyed by UUID with retries and backoff; crops copied with rsync
decision.why: Idempotent upserts make at-least-once delivery safe, which is the realistic guarantee over a flaky link. rsync with --partial keeps interrupted files so the next run resumes. Nothing in the camera loop waits on the network.

alternatives.name: MQTT to a broker on the laptop
alternatives.tradeoff: Push-based and near real time, but you still need local buffering for outages and a broker running all season.

alternatives.name: Wired PoE instead of Wi-Fi
alternatives.tradeoff: The Pi docs list PoE support on several models with a HAT; one cable fixes both power and network, at the cost of running it outdoors.

steps.delegate: In Python, write a sync worker: every 5 minutes, select up to 500 unsynced visits, POST them as JSON to a small FastAPI receiver on the laptop that upserts by uuid into its own SQLite, mark synced on HTTP 200, exponential backoff with jitter on failure. rsync the crops directory. Tests: receiver gets the same batch twice and stores it once; network cut mid-batch; device offline for a day then catches up.
verify: Kill the network mid-upload and confirm the laptop ends with exactly the device's row count, no duplicates
Leave the device offline for 24 h and measure time to catch up after reconnecting
Track sync lag (now minus newest synced visit) for a week and report the median and max

steps.title: Power it for a whole season
steps.learn: Measure, do not guess: average watts across a day sets the battery or solar size. Raspberry Pi docs say all models need a 5.1 V supply and low-quality supplies can corrupt storage, which in a feeder means a lost log. Heat inside a sealed box causes throttling.

decision.choice: Mains power through an outdoor-rated supply (or PoE), with measured average power logged for a week
decision.why: A Pi running a camera all day is not a small battery load. Mains power removes a whole class of failures so the season of data is complete; the measured watts tell you later whether solar is realistic.

alternatives.name: Battery plus solar panel
alternatives.tradeoff: No cable, but cloudy weeks drain it, and you need measured daily energy plus margin; expect gaps in winter.

alternatives.name: ESP32 with PIR wake from deep sleep
alternatives.tradeoff: Fits battery power, but on-device classification is limited; you may only capture and upload images for the laptop to classify.

steps.delegate: Write a small Python health logger for the Pi: every minute record vcgencmd measure_temp, CPU load, free disk, SQLite size and uptime to the same database, and raise a local flag file when disk is above 80% or temperature is high. Add a daily cleanup that deletes synced crops older than N days.
verify: Measure average power over 24 h with a USB power meter and write down watt-hours per day
Check the board logs for under-voltage or throttling warnings after a week outdoors
Confirm disk use stays flat over a week with the cleanup job running

steps.title: Measure accuracy on your own captures
steps.learn: Label a sample of visits yourself (species or no bird or unsure) using a field guide. Compute top-1 and top-3 accuracy, per-species precision and recall, and a confusion matrix. Frames from one visit are near-duplicates, so split by visit and by date, never by frame.

decision.choice: Hand-label about 300 visits sampled across weeks and times of day, held out by date from any training data
decision.why: Random frame splits leak the same bird into train and test and overstate accuracy. Sampling across weeks covers changing light, plumage and species mix, and keeps the test set honest if you later distill a student.

alternatives.name: Trust model confidence as a proxy
alternatives.tradeoff: No labeling work, but confidence is not accuracy; confident mistakes on lookalike species go unnoticed.

alternatives.name: Score on NABirds instead
alternatives.tradeoff: Large and expert-labeled, but it measures the model on curated photos, not on your feeder; use only as a secondary check.

steps.delegate: Write a labeling tool (Python, a simple local web page or Jupyter widget) that shows a visit's best crop and records species, no bird, or unsure into a labels table. Add an evaluation script that computes top-1, top-3, per-species precision and recall, a confusion matrix, and accuracy by hour of day and by week, using perceptual hashing to drop near-duplicate crops.
verify: Label at least 300 visits and report top-1 and top-3 accuracy with the count per species
List the 3 most confused species pairs and look at 5 examples of each
Confirm no visit appears in both a training set and the test set (check by visit UUID and date)

steps.title: Privacy and safety check
steps.learn: The camera identifies birds, not people. Neighbors, passers-by and windows may enter the frame. Do not store faces: drop any frame where the detector sees a person before it is saved or synced, and mask the street out of view. Feeding wildlife has local rules and hygiene guidance; the app is only a helper.

decision.choice: Discard frames with a person detection on the device, mask non-feeder regions, and never upload raw video
decision.why: The detector already runs, so a person filter costs nothing extra, and dropping frames on the device means people never reach the laptop or any published chart. Crops of the perch only are what the project needs.

alternatives.name: Blur people instead of dropping frames
alternatives.tradeoff: Keeps more bird frames, but blurring can fail and the original still exists in memory or the pre-roll clip.

alternatives.name: Aim the camera so no public space is visible
alternatives.tradeoff: The strongest fix where possible; may limit placement, so combine it with the filter.

steps.delegate: Add a privacy filter: write triggered clips and bursts to a tmpfs (RAM) folder first; run the COCO detector on every frame of them, and if any shows a person above a low threshold, delete the clip and burst and log only a counter (no image). Move to disk only when all frames pass. Add a static mask that blacks out non-feeder regions before saving. Tests: sample images and clips with people never reach disk; counter increments.
verify: Walk past the feeder 10 times and confirm no frame of you was saved or synced, only the counter changed
Check the mask on saved crops: no street, window or neighbor property visible
Check your local wildlife agency's guidance on feeding birds and feeder cleaning, and note the source you used
Confirm published charts make no claims about rare species presence or population (the model card rules this out)

steps.title: Test it outside for a season and publish visit charts
steps.learn: Run the feeder for a season. Charts are visits per species by hour of day and by week, with confidence filtered and low-confidence events shown as unknown. Track the system too: uptime, triggers per day, false-trigger rate, sync lag. Gaps in uptime must show as gaps, not as zero birds.
verify: Report uptime percent for the season and mark every outage on the charts
Publish charts of visits per species by hour and by week, with the accuracy from your labels next to them
Report false triggers per day at the start and end of the season
Re-label 50 visits from the last month and compare accuracy with the first month

steps.title: Write it up
steps.learn: Four parts: (1) the one question; (2) numbers for every claim with the device, model version and command; (3) why the surprising results happened, for example a species the model kept confusing or a time of day with many false triggers; (4) assumptions and what this does not prove.
verify: The write-up states the one question at the top
Every claim has a number with the device, model file and command or script that produced it
At least one surprising result is explained with examples (crops, confusion pairs, trigger logs)
An assumptions section says what this does not prove (one feeder, one season, visits not population, label noise)
